speechtext: The House resumed, from Monday, May 5, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bussieres (for the Minister of Finance) that Bill C-6, to revise the Bank Act, to amend the Quebec Savings Banks Act and the Bank of Canada Act, to establish the Canadian Payments Association and to amend other acts in consequence thereof, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, I have just a few minutes to finish the remarks I began last evening, when 1 spoke of the difficulties faced by many businesses in Canada in financing their operations, particularly small and medium-sized businesses, and the ends to which some of them have to go. This whole matter of financing a business is not very well understood. I am sorry to say I do not think it is very
Bank Act
well understood by the banks as well as some of the people in business.
Before foreign exchange rates began to fluctuate, we had situations where it was easier and cheaper to finance inventories outside of Canada than in Canada. In other words, suppliers came to potential Canadian customers asking them to give them a year or two order for a product and they would put that inventory on the shelves at approximately half the rate that was available in Canada. There is an area here where the Canadian banks could move in and perform a service to help many of our businesses retain that sort of financing within Canada.
When you commit yourself to a year or two years' supply at fixed financing terms to someone outside the country, it leaves the businessman with not too much flexibility. It does not give him an opportunity to look around. He is enticed into this type of arrangement by the fact that he can get very low interest rates. I notice as well with the EX-IM Bank in the United States that many times American suppliers will come in and in fact supply a product that is already made in Canada. However, the financing rates are considerably lower than what can be had here. Consequently the Canadian consumer will make his purchase from the United States rather than from a Canadian supplier because he can get cheaper financing.
As we consider this act-and I repeat that I hope we can handle it with a reasonable amount of dispatch in the days and weeks ahead-I hope we will be able to leave the banks free to enter into more types of financing of inventories. I would like to see a consortium of our banks get together to handle collectively some exporting for the small and medium-sized business sector of our economy. There is an opening there.
In my business experience, I have done a little bit of exporting. On a couple of occasions I had to go to a finance company in order to export to a customer in the Caribbean. There is an opportunity here for Canadian banks to move into that area and stimulate that part of our economy which employs the largest number of people in our labour force.
That, Mr. Speaker, concludes the remarks I have to make. As I say, I hope we can move with a good deal of dispatch and see this bill passed on to the other House in good order.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege, indeed an honour, to be able to discuss this afternoon the bill before us.
Bill C-6, which will revise the Bank Act and amend the Quebec Savings Banks Act and the Bank of Canada Act as well as establish the Canadian Payments Association, is clearly the most important piece of long-term legislation with which this Parliament will have to deal. It will establish the legislative framework within which the Canadian banking system will develop over the next ten or, as we have seen lately, perhaps 13 years. Thus, it is of crucial importance that we consider very carefully the provisions of this bill and their long-term implications for the development of Canada.

May 6, 1980
Bank Act
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian banking system plays a central role in the performance of the Canadian economy. It develops in large part the major payments mechanism facilitating transactions in our mixed market system. In holding the great majority of Canadian chequing accounts and savings deposits the banks assume a special responsibility in managing the nation's money supply. But the banks' most important function in terms of long-range development of the Canadian economy is to provide for the allocation of financial capital among alternative investment opportunities.
The Canadian economy is faced with a number of very serious structural problems as we enter the 1980s. Our balance of payments has deteriorated to unprecedented levels. Our SI 1.5 billion trade deficit in finished manufactured goods portrays a colossal failure on the part of the government to implement a foreign trade policy and domestic industrial strategy consistent with the long-term development of our economy. We are becoming increasingly dependent on the export of primary resources that provide expanded opportunities for the employment of foreign capital in Canada while our manufacturing sector, which provides the greatest opportunity for increasing the employment of Canadians, slips slowly into oblivion, I am sorry to say. The key, high-technology sectors of our economy continue to be dominated by foreign interests. As a result, research and new-product development is inadequately funded. But more important, there has been no attempt to rationalize the Canadian industrial structure to make these industries more competitive in the world economy.
The solutions to these problems are clear to most Canadians. We need efficient, world-scale industries. We need to increase Canadian control in order to stop the drain of financial resources out of Canada. We need to encourage import substitution and to develop efficient capital markets to provide the financial support required to rationalize and to modernize Canadian industry. The Canadian banking system can play a key role in achieving these national objectives and that is what makes the revision to the Bank Act before us for debate today so crucially important.
As the major financial intermediaries in the Canadian economy, the banks receive deposits and lend out huge amounts of capital. Will the Bank Act ensure that these pools of capital will be used to support Canadian business, to promote Canadian industrial development and reverse the trend toward foreign domination? I have my doubts, Mr. Speaker, but let us consider for a moment the proposed legislation.
Revising the legislation governing the Canadian banking system appears to be a ritual engaging this House every ten years or so. In my reading of the record one of the most clearly stated objectives of this ritual in the past has been to increase the level of competition in Canadian banking. This time around it appears that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Mac-Eachen) has decided that competition can best be promoted by allowing foreign banks access to the Canadian economy.
This seems a rather curious decision to me. What is even
more curious is why the chartered banks have not objected,
indeed, why they have agreed so readily to allow foreign banks access to the Canadian capital market. The government thinks such access will increase competition in this highly concentrated sector of the economy. But, Mr. Speaker, the banks know better. And so, too, should the members of this House, especially those members more experienced than I, and in particular those members who have debated this very act over the past few years. As a new member of Parliament representing the concerns of my constituents about the effectiveness of federal government policy, I find it difficult to reconcile the objective of increasing competition in the banking system as expressed by some members of this House with the actual performance of the banks themselves.
In 1954 the four largest chartered banks held $8.7 billion in total assets. This represented 76.8 per cent of total chartered bank assets. By 1979-25 years later-the assets held by the same four banks had grown to $182.6 billion, representing 77.7 per cent of total chartered bank assets. Therefore, over the past 25 years there has been virtually no change in the concentration of assets among Canadian chartered banks.
The credibility of our legislative commitment to ensure greater competition in banking is most seriously questioned by the performance record of the chartered banks in concentrating corporate profits. In 1954, the four largest chartered banks received $51.8 million in profits before taxes. This represented 70.6 per cent of all chartered bank profits before taxes. By 1979 the pre-tax profits received by the four largest chartered banks had grown to $1.1 billion, representing 80.6 per cent of all chartered bank profits before taxes.
In spite of the well-intentioned objectives expressed by so many members of this House, Mr. Speaker, the chartered banks in Canada are no more competitive today than they were 25 years ago. Indeed, a strong case can be made for them being less competitive today. I am afraid that the hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) was all too correct when he suggested the other night that what we were doing here in debating this bill was akin to laying down the rules for the manufacture of horse collars in an age of jet propulsion, rockets and advanced electronics. Still, we are told that this new legislation will increase competition and the chartered banks are on record as agreeing with this. I want to suggest that the kind of competition the banks are talking about is definitely not the kind of competition I have heard discussed by members of this House. But I will return to that point later.
First let me say something about the source of this new competition in the Canadian banking system. The new Bank Act will allow foreign banks to establish banking subsidiaries in Canada. This section of the bill provides very little in the way of federal leadership. In fact, it validates and formalizes a trend which has been growing for some time. Once again, like the banks' involvement in auto leasing, we act after the fact rather than before. We are followers, not leaders. Foreign banks have significantly expanded their activities in Canada over the past decade. The Minister of State, Finance (Mr. Bussieres) very briefly indicated the number of financial affiliates of foreign banks the government has been able to identify.
May 6, 1980

The minister also indicated that the total assets of these affiliates reporting to the Bank of Canada exceeds $6.4 billion.
Mr. Speaker, there are a number of things that are very disturbing about this entire question of foreign banks operating in Canada. First, we seem to be responding after the fact in providing a legislative framework for the activities of foreign banks in the Canadian economy and, furthermore, we are justifying this belated action on the grounds that subsidiaries of foreign banks will increase competition in Canada. However, the government has not provided the members of this House with any comprehensive information on, or analysis of, the activities of currently operating financial affiliates of foreign banks in this country. We in fact know very little about their activities.
I must agree with the comments made in this House last evening by members sitting on the Conservative benches that these foreign banks will not necessarily be operating in the best interests of Canada or Canadians. The question whether these foreign banks will be offering services in small communities throughout Canada and especially northern Canada was posed. Will these foreign banks or their subsidiaries be offering services to the small entrepreneur in the Canadian context? Will they be providing financial services to everyday working Canadians? I suspect not. 1 suspect, as the hon. member indicated last evening, that these will be metropolitan banks, perhaps skimming off the best deals in the resource and industrial sectors, and that they will do little for the new small Canadian banks becoming established in Canada today, such as the bank in my own province, the Bank of British Columbia. Of course, credit unions and caisses populaires are already under undue disadvantages as compared with our chartered banks. No, I do not feel we need the Bank of America in Canada today.
Frankly, 1 am concerned about the deterioration of our economic performance in the 1970s, and it appears that we can expect these trends to continue, at least in the early 1980s. Regional disparities and structural weaknesses in our economy have become worse, not better, over the past few years. Our manufacturing sector continues to decline, employing only 19 per cent of the nation's labour force in 1979. In 1970, nine years ago, 21 per cent of Canada's exports were manufactured goods. Today they represent 10 per cent. Our balance of trade deficit in manufactured goods stood at $3 billion in 1970, whereas last year it was $11.5 billion. In the past five years $13.8 billion in dividends and interest payments were drained out of Canada. An additional $8.5 billion left Canada in management consulting fees, patent fees and licence and copyright fees.
I suggest that these are very serious matters. Yet we are asked to approve those provisions of Bill C-6 which would allow for the expanded activities of foreign banks in the Canadian economy without knowing the role financial affiliates of foreign banks have played or can be expected to play, first, in improving or contributing to a further deterioration of
Bank Act
our manufacturing sector; second, in facilitating foreign penetration in Canadian industry; and third, in improving or contributing to a further decline in our balance of international payments. These are questions of concern to all Canadians, and this legislation fails to address these concerns.
We are told that we are debating the question of competition in Canadian banking. I suggest that we are debating much more than that: we are debating the future of the Canadian manufacturing industry and the future of our balance of payments. As all of us in this House know, major changes are now required in our manufacturing industry in an effort to improve the status of our balance of payments situation in Canada.
To return to the point concerning the differences between our conception of competition and that of the chartered banks, the Minister of State for Finance, in moving the motion for second reading of Bill C-6, indicated that this latest revision of the Bank Act would have the effect of increasing bank competition and thus lead to better service for consumers and business borrowers requiring credit. There are, of course, no a priori reasons, let alone historic evidence, to indicate that these results will follow automatically. The large Canadian chartered banks are today among the world's largest. They have already achieved the economies associated with large scale banking enterprise. The challenge to us is to ensure that those economies are passed on to Canadian consumers and Canadian businesses. Unfortunately, Bill C-6 will fall far short of this objective.
The point is that the large Canadian chartered banks have little to fear from a handful of specialized subsidiaries of foreign banks. The chartered banks know this, and that is why they support this legislation. The kind of competition the chartered banks are looking for in this bill is the leverage that it will afford them in gaining access to foreign capital markets.
This was stated quite succinctly, if not unwittingly, by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology (Mr. Simmons) when he said just last week, and I quote: "It will mean that our banks will have access to foreign markets." It remains to be seen how this increased activity of our chartered banks overseas will benefit Canadian consumers, home owners and businesses.
I suggest that we are debating much more than a series of revisions to the Bank Act in this the Thirty-second Parliament. We are debating what may in effect become an international charter for the large scale banks in Canada, a proclamation of the increasingly international ambitions of our chartered banks and what may be a growth commitment to international allocation of financial resources on the basis of greatest profit.
The chartered banks have been granted a privileged position in our economy by the people of Canada. They exercise a tremendous influence over the allocation of financial resources in the economic system and thus have a profound impact on our ability to achieve important national goals. As representatives, it is our responsibility to ensure that the legislative framework we provide for the activities of the chartered banks

May 6, 1980
Bank Act
promotes behaviour consistent with the achievement of our national goals.
One cannot overemphasize that the chartered banks should be encouraged by this House to provide funding for socially responsible areas. The banks ought to assist us in our attempts at developing an industrial strategy for Canada. The banks should assist us in obtaining the national goals of a serious, well rounded employment strategy for Canada, regional development, improvements in transportation and communication, and a move toward more Canadian control in the affairs of Petro-Canada, a principle and concept that in the last election the people of Canada indicated they supported, and supported very seriously and strongly.
Will the banks assist us in developing a serious housing policy for Canada? Will the banks assist us in providing opportunities for small entrepreneurs, encouraging them and enabling them to enter into new and foreign markets? Will the banks assist our agricultural sector? Will they provide assistance to the native people on reserves across the country to enable them to take advantage of opportunities that they are creating every day?
In considering the entire question of competition and the banking system I am somewhat surprised that the government has placed its emphasis on increasing the role of foreign financial institutions in Canada, for if there has been one source of increased competition in the Canadian financial capital market during the 1970s we have just come through, it has come from the growth of wholly Canadian non-bank financial intermediaries, particularly credit unions and caisses populaires.
During the 1970s public confidence in big business fell significantly, but that was not the case with credit unions. Between 1967 and 1977 the total assets of banks and trust companies grew at an annual compound growth rate of 15 per cent and 16 per cent respectively, but the assets of credit unions increased by 19.2 per cent. In 1967, 4,308,000 Canadians belonged to credit unions or caisses populaires. Their membership represented 56 per cent of the labour force in Canada. By 1978 membership had nearly doubled, to 8,318,000 Canadians, or 78.4 per cent of Canada's labour force.
This growth performance among credit unions has occurred in spite of numerous legislative obstacles which have hampered the development of non-bank financial intermediaries. For example, the Financial Administration Act prevents the federal government from maintaining deposits with credit unions. Through that act the federal government discriminates against credit unions in favour of chartered banks. Chartered banks are also favoured by the provisions of the Small Businesses Loans Act, the Farm Credit Act and the Fisheries Improvement Loans Act, all of which require credit unions to register individually in order to be able to provide services under those acts. [DOT]
All members of the House, I am sure, are aware of the
inequity created in the marketplace by the Small Loans Act in
that it does not apply to chartered banks. By imposing a 12 per cent interest rate ceiling on loans under $1,500, obviously it severely limits the flexibility of credit unions to provide revolving credit to their members. Chartered banks are, of course, unhindered by this legislation and can provide this service through direct loans or through their credit card operations.
The point is, Mr. Speaker, if we are really serious about promoting Canadian enterprise and increasing competition in the financial capital market, then we should not be making it easier for foreign banks to operate in Canada. We should be considering a comprehensive revision of all financial legislation that inhibits the establishment of more Canadian banks, the expansion and diversification of credit unions and caisses populaires as well as the development of alternative financial institutions such as postal savings banks.
Mr. Speaker, over the past few years, and especially since becoming a member of Parliament, I have become increasingly aware of the many problems individual Canadians, and especially Canadian businesses, have had in dealing with the chartered banks. This is an area of banking we tend to dismiss as unimportant, but I would suggest it requires far more attention than it has received in the past or will receive in this legislation.
The chartered banks are monolithic, secretive institutions. We need to know more about their operations, but information is often not available or very difficult to obtain. In general, chartered banks are too nervous with small companies, and often loans are recalled prematurely. If a business requires additional short-term credit instead of increasing the loan, some banks prefer to use overdrafts which end up costing the small business in the range of 25 per cent to 30 per cent. Numerous cases exist where a businessman was making regular payments and a demand loan was called by his bank. These factors along with highly variable interest rates make it especially difficult for businesses to plan for even the near future, let alone do any long-term economic planning.
Decisions by the banks to alter the terms of credit or call in a loan add to the uncertainty and risks of small business. A significant number of bankruptcies could be avoided if there were better communications between small companies and banks and if banks were required to be more accountable for their decision to withdraw financial support to business ventures.
In a recent study of consumer satisfaction with financial services, 21 per cent of more than 1,000 respondents indicated that in the previous two years they had one or more experiences with financial or insurance services with which they were highly dissatisfied. Sixty per cent of those reporting dissatisfaction indicated they had had five or more bad experiences during that time period. This does little toward improving the investment climate for entrepreneurs interested in Canada's future.
Among the highly dissatisfied purchasers of financial services who cited financial institutions as most unsatisfactory, chartered banks received the highest percentage at 32.6 while credit unions received the lowest percentage at 4.3. Trust
May 6, 1980

companies, credit card services and consumer loan or finance companies fell in between these extremes.
The most frequently cited reasons for consumer dissatisfaction with financial services were as follows:
The service was provided in a careless and unprofessional manner.
And the person-
-was treated like an object rather than as an individual.
Another survey of 16,000 businesses across Canada, although indicating that Canada's chartered banks are providing better than reasonable service to a majority of small and medium-sized businesses, highlighted a number of serious problems. For example, many small and medium-sized businesses are not receiving the quality of service enjoyed by older, established businesses. About 75 per cent of the operators of firms in business more than ten years believe their bank managers understand the nature of their enterprises, versus only 65 per cent of those in business less than four years. Again, I suggest, this does very little toward encouraging the new ideas and energies to enter the marketplace.
The survey also indicated that local bank managers are not visiting clients on a regular basis. Sixty-two per cent of the businesses surveyed had never been visited. This kind of contact undoubtedly plays a significant role in the bank manager's understanding of the small businessman and his problems.
In Saskatchewan, for example, 77 per cent of the respondents had been visited and 78 per cent were confident their manager understood the nature of their business, while in Ontario only 60 per cent of the businesses surveyed had been visited by their bank manager, and in that province only 69 per cent of the respondents believed their bankers understood clearly their operations.
These are all more or less serious problems facing small and medium-sized business in Canada. But a somewhat different problem exists in the very special relationship our chartered banks have cultivated with big business, and in particular the multinational corporations that dominate the Canadian economy. In a very real sense it has been easier for a Kaiser Resources Ltd. to borrow hundreds of millions of dollars from Canadian chartered banks to finance the takeover of an Ashland Oil Ltd. than it has been for many independent Canadian manufacturers to obtain financing for their own industrial expansion.
The historical record is all too clear on this crucial point. The chartered banks in Canada have played a central role in the sell-out of the Canadian economy. Who would better realize this than the present Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gray), author of a very important report seven years ago on the foreign takeover of Canadian industry. We on this side of the House congratulate the hon. member on his present appointment and look forward to his proposals for redressing this historical error in our country's industrial underdevelopment.
I am afraid that Canadians hold a fairly low opinion of their chartered banks, perhaps not as low as the oil companies but low nonetheless. Oh, they know they are financially sound,
Bank Act
secure and very profitable, but they seriously question whether the chartered banks are conducting their business in a way that fulfils the public trust which we have placed in them. My colleague the hon. member from Comox-Powell River (Mr. Skelly) has pointed to the much broader commitment to disclosure among large banks in the United States and the glaring deficiencies in the legislation under debate which, although it is an improvement, falls short of what Canadians expect in the way of reasonable information and protection.
My colleague the hon. member from Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae) has raised the serious question of interest rate spreads and price discrimination by the chartered banks. How is it, Mr. Speaker, that in 1980 we can pass legislation that is silent on the "rule of 78" and other such discriminatory practices?
The banks tell us that without a penalty on the prepayment of loans and mortgages, their profits would be squeezed, that they might even lose money! Yet credit unions have been operating without penalties for years and they manage to survive. Indeed, they have grown and become more popular.
I fear, Mr. Speaker, that the Canadian people have every right to be concerned about what we do here today. I have been discussing the financial leasing provisions of the new Bank Act with many automobile dealers in my riding. Recently I was in receipt of a letter from the Canadian Federation of Independent Business indicating that in a survey which they recently conducted with over 55,000 independent business people, 67 per cent were against the idea of banks becoming involved in the automobile leasing business. They are concerned, without having seen the regulations to be prescribed by the governor in council, that this may not only create a conflict of interest for the banks, but may also seriously reduce competition in certain segments of the leasing field over the long run.
Evidence would indicate that in the field of leasing we can expect to be falling behind those activities in the state of California. I understand that nearly 40 per cent of the automobile business in the state of California is now done through the leasing business. You can see that this, then, will probably be increasing in Canada in the years ahead. We can see that banks are interested in getting a piece of that action, and I suggest we would not be doing the independent dealers any good by following suit. Although the banks have indicated that becoming involved in the traditional leasing business is not their aim, I think either yesterday or the day before evidence was discussed in the House by other members that indeed it would appear the banks intend to get into it in much the same way as traditional leasing companies.
The hon. member for Edmonton West has pointed to the failure of this act to define the business of banking. I would suggest that it also fails to define clearly what the government means by competition in the banking system.
I previously mentioned that the chartered banks shared a dubious distinction with the oil companies-Canadians distrust them both. It is clear that we know little more about the

May 6, 1980
Bank Act
internal dynamics of the banking system than we do about the oil industry. Because of the privileged position of the chartered banks in the Canadian economy, Canadians have every right to know more, to have a better understanding of the role that our chartered banks play in the Canadian economy.
Other countries view the central role of their banks in the economy far more seriously than we have in the past, particularly if this bill is any indication. The provisions of Bill C-6 restricting public participation in the ownership of chartered banks denies the public an opportunity to participate actively in the banking industry. Such participation would not only provide a new source of competition in Canadian banking, but, to use a much-used phrase, it would provide a window on the banking industry which would allow Canadians better to assess the performance of their banking system.
I am sure this proposal will cause some concern for the members to my right and, of course, will barely arouse the members across the way who are determined to bring Canada's banking system into the nineteenth century with this legislation.
The proposal to promote public participation in banking is anything but unique. In West Germany the local levels of Government wholly own nearly all the savings banks. There are 675 such banks in West Germany with a total of over 20,000 local branch offices or agencies. While most of these savings banks are of a small size, taken together their liabilities exceed all but the four largest commercial banks in West Germany.
The West German banking system is two-tiered in nature. The top tier contains large commercial banks which are privately owned. These banks engage mainly in wholesale banking, lending to large businesses and owning equity in large industrial corporations, and financing these activities by issuing debt obligations. Retail banking, accepting chequing and savings deposits and making small personal loans and mortgages, is the almost exclusive preserve of the publicly-owned savings banks.
In France nearly all of the commercial banks operating at a national level are majority or wholly owned by the government. Following World War II the three largest banks in France-the Societe Generale, the Banque Nationale de Paris and the Credit Lyonnais-were nationalized by the government.
In the United Kingdom the government, through its department of national savings, operates the National Savings Bank. This bank has over 20 million active savings accounts representing deposit liabilities of close to three billion pounds. The bank has no premises, a marked contrast to our marble towers of Bay Street, but it operates through local post office branches throughout the United Kingdom. All other commercial banks in the United Kingdom are privately owned.
This very brief survey of different banking systems simply serves to highlight the narrowness of purpose, the neglect of national economic priorities and the lack of vision represented by this latest revision of the Bank Act. 1 began my comments
by comparing the Bank Act to the laying down of rules for the manufacture of horse collars. It will be a great disappointment to the Canadian people that after years of parliamentary deliberations, after hundreds of thousands of man-hours spent debating this bill, they cannot at least expect better horse collars.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I take great pleasure in saying a few words on the Bank Act. 1 will not attempt to give any high-faluting essay or speech on this very complicated act. Rather, I will try to speak in the language of an ordinary citizen and state what we expect from a banking system in this modern age, and to check whether or not we are now satisfied with what we are receiving from our banking system. I will do that by referring to a number of items.
First I want to deal with the matter of agriculture to the extent it is affected by the Bank Act. This act is of concern to many farmers because a section of it deals with loans to borrowers and security for such. That section is used largely by banks when making loans to packers and farmers. When I refer to "farmers", I include ranchers and various forms of agriculture. I cannot understand why the act sets out priority of rights to certain farmers and denies rights to other farmers who are also producing food for the benefit of the people. For instance, it provides priority of rights to growers of perishable products which are direct products of the soil and to the producers of dairy products. The formula which can be worked out from that would indicate that the maximum loan probably would be in the vicinity of $20,000.
I have a question for the hon. minister which I hope he will pursue to ascertain a reasonable answer or else change the legislation. Why leave out livestock producers, as one example? Why not include all producers, if we are to include any, and give them all the same privileges under the Bank Act? This making fish of one and flesh of another in such a vital matter as credit is not right. It will hurt the country and those deprived of those priorities such as livestock producers.
There should be no upper limit. Surely the banks can determine if the value is there, if the security is there or if the equity is there, without our telling them that they have to put on an upper limit in regard to loans to agriculture. An upper limit of $20,000 certainly is not satisfactory for the livestock business or for many other forms of agriculture. A level of $250,000 might be more sensible, but why should there be any upper limit? Are the banks themselves not able to determine the extent to which they can lend? Doing this by blanket legislation will hurt many operations. I cannot see why we, sitting in the House of Commons, think that we can make loans better than those who are doing it day by day and checking the security being offered.
Another item which bothers me very greatly is the security offered to packers in this country. They use the word "procedure" and not the word "purchase". Packers take in hundreds of cattle, probably thousands of cattle or sheep or hogs, but let us deal with cattle for the moment. They "procure" them but
May 6, 1980

they have not yet secured "ownership" of them. They still belong to the farmer until he is paid for those cattle; they still belong to the livestock dealer, the livestock operator or the rancher. But under the present wording of the act, the packer may use the cattle of other people to secure a much larger loan than he normally could secure. If there has to be foreclosure, the foreclosure is then on the cattle that did not belong to the packer. He procured them but he has not yet purchased them. 1 suggest that we change the word in the act, because there is a great principle involved, to the word "purchase". Once the packer has purchased the cattle, then he should be able to use them as security or equity or for any purpose he sees fit. Surely he should not use my 1,000 head of cattle or the livestock of any other producer for his own security before he has paid us for them. This is not fair when it results in foreclosure.
1 suggest we will be increasing the number of such foreclosures by encouraging bankers, and probably many others who have procured the product but have not yet paid for it, to follow this practice. I would like to see the word "purchase" put in the act, or perhaps there is a better word. This item should certainly be discussed very carefully in the committee.
Another thing that bothers many individuals in this country is the trend toward monopolies. I enjoyed the address by the hon. member of the New Democratic Party who just spoke, but I completely disagree with him regarding the nationalization of banks or of anything else. 1 have yet to see the apple tree that grows more apples because it is nationalized. I suggest that the nationalization of an apple tree would result in the producer getting less, because there will be more civil servants working out rules and regulations as to how an apple tree can be kept, who can pick the apples, when, where and why.
Nationalization has its place, but this country was built, with all due respect to hon. members of the NDP, on the free enterprise system, the credit system and on the system of individual effort, not on nationalization and not by the government. It was built rather as a result of thousands of individuals who were willing to risk their shirts, using everything they had, in fact, sometimes only the strength of their backs, to go out and develop this country. Now because we have so much development it is suggested that we should start nationalizing this and that.
The banks can do a job without nationalization. Certain changes should be made, and I hope some will be made, but I am concerned about the trend we are moving toward, and that is the back door way of putting monopoly in our banks. There is a danger in this bill that this may very well take place.
Let us look at the part of this measure which is supposed to provide for competition. I heard a banker say, not longer ago than today, that this item was being put in so that banks could compete with automobile dealers and other businesses. Surely that is not why we are bringing competition in under the Bank Act. My understanding is that this will provide competition
Bank Act
with and among other people doing the same business-the lending of money and the accepting of deposits. Surely we are not going to stretch the meaning of this word "competition" to enable bankers to compete with ice cream parlours.
When you walk into some of our drugstores today you do not know whether you are in a general store, an ice cream parlour, a restaurant, a hardware shop or a drugstore. They have everything in them. We should not start this with our banks. When there is a good thing going, such as with ice cream, under this legislation they could get into the ice cream business. I do not blame bankers for wanting to get into these businesses, but they are not in that field. Bankers see a good thing in the leasing of automobiles, trucks and heavy equipment so they now want to get into the leasing business, the actual merchandising of these products.
Let us follow this through. If banks are allowed to do this, they could get into the leasing business, dealing with perhaps just 100 trucks. They could fix the rates for leasing those 100 trucks, and that rate could go up or down as the banks see fit, within limits, with the result that the people who own the merchandise, garages and small dealers, would have to adjust accordingly. This could very well reduce their margin of profit to the point where they could not stay in business.
When a bank lends money to a dealer today it does so on the basis of the trustworthiness of that individual, the type of business he is operating, his assets, etc. If a man is in the business of leasing these pieces of equipment to individuals, whether it is one truck or 100 trucks, the banks base their loans on something else entirely. In this way the banks are interfering with the livelihood of others because they could well reduce their own interest rate to the point where the small operator could not stay in business.
Most of these small operators do business in small towns rather than in big places like Ottawa, Toronto, Edmonton, Calgary, Red Deer, although they are there too. They operate in places like Strathmore, Airdrie, Drumheller, a small city of 7,000 people, Rumsey, Claresholm, that type of town right across this country. If these people cannot continue in the leasing business and make a reasonable profit, they will move out of those small towns. If they cannot meet their requirements and their commitments, what will happen? I suggest there will be foreclosures and the banks will take back the vehicles. Where will these people then go? I suggest they will move to the big cities and again there will be a trend toward monopoly and centralization.
Even if someone is able to meet all his requirements and commitments, who will carry out the repairs and maintenance now being done by these automobile dealers in our small centres? If we want to put another nail in the coffins of our small towns let us continue with this proposal, because it is just another step to drive those people in our small towns out of business.
I saw this happen in relation to the machinery business. They started with one thing and then went on and on, and the first thing we knew was that in order to get parts we had to go to the big cities of Calgary, Edmonton or Regina in the west.

May 6, 1980
Bank Act
When a farmer needs parts he needs them now, not tomorrow and not the next day. The farmer cannot depend on the sun shining every day; he needs the services immediately. I suggest that the minister take a careful look at this idea of permitting our banks to get into this business of leasing, as this is something that could lead to monopolies and the destruction of our small cities.
This is not the kind of competition we expect in relation to banks. We do not expect that they should be in competition with automobile dealers and other merchants with whom the banks now do business, but rather with other banks.
This country is pretty well served by those in the garage business and in auto dealerships. They give a pretty fair deal to our people, providing maintenance and help when it is needed in this day of stress. When a farmer's truck breaks down in the midst of harvest, the small dealer in our towns will on many occasions lend the farmer his own or another truck. It is a service which our farmers and our people appreciate. Let us not kill small business in our towns. I am afraid that if this clause is put into effect it will lead to more bankruptcies.
There was discussion the other day about the figure of 546 bankruptcies in 1978. I wonder how many of those bankruptcies occurred due to foreclosure. I wish that figure were available. Sometimes foreclosure is made without heart, even though there are many warmhearted bankers. In many cases a little consideration and a little help would keep these small businessmen in business.
When I have a complaint with my garage or automobile dealer, I contact the consumer affairs department of the provincial government and they look into the matter for me. If there is provision in the Bank Act for the banks to take over leasing, to whom do I complain, other than to my MP or my MLA, who may not have the wherewithal to carry out the research necessary to determine if there is gouging or something of this nature.
Let us not mix up our jurisdictions. I suggest that the banks stay in the business of lending money and otherwise stay out of small business. Banks on the whole are doing very well today. They are not on the poverty line. There should not be any provisions in the Bank Act which will be detrimental to small business, small towns or small cities. The amount of money made by our automobile dealers and such businesses is not out of line. This clause seems to be a good thing, but the small dealers in our small towns sometimes bid on large contracts in order to stay alive and to remain in that small town. I would like to say that all leases are not necessarily foolproof, even though they may be arranged by banks, and there will be some incidents of foreclosure. Let us not kill our small towns by putting this service in the hands of our bankers.
Then there is the matter of credit cards. More and more banks want to get into the credit card business for the profit it offers. I suggest that the charges for credit cards are unfair in many cases to the customer who pays cash. Hon. members should not think that it is only the rich who pay cash. Many of
our hard-working people buy things only with the money they may have available from their pay cheque. These people live from pay cheque to pay cheque and do not rely on credit cards. They do not mortgage their future with credit cards. When we provide for the extravagant use of credit cards, somebody is paying for them and in many cases it is the cash customer. This matter should be reviewed very carefully and if it is the cash customer who is paying, then remedial action should be taken.
The next point I would like to mention is the matter of interference by banks with individual accounts. I do not think this procedure is widespread. However, some four or five years ago I had a small savings account at one of the chartered banks. I did not use the account because it was a savings account which was held in trust. After I had had the account for some two or three years, I took my bank book in to get it balanced. At that time I noticed there was a service charge of $2. When I asked the clerk about the service charge, after indicating that I had not used the account and that the money had simply sat there for the use of the banks for two or three years, the clerk said, "You are being charged because you did not use the money." 1 instructed that clerk at the desk to take my book back to the manager and to tell him to take the service charge off. I felt that he had no authority under the Bank Act to charge me that $2. The clerk came back after 15 minutes and returned my book to me without the service charge. I forthwith removed my money from that particular chartered bank.
That is gouging, Mr. Speaker. Why should I be charged a service charge when I do not use my account and after the bank has had the use of my money? It was not a current account. Too often banks are using every possible excuse to charge for their services, and sometimes the charge is exorbitant. I recently saw a sign on a bank which said, "Fifty cents to cash a cheque, unless you are an old age pensioner". I would like to know what is the tremendous amount of work involved in cashing a cheque. Banks do not cash a cheque unless they are certain that it is good.
The Bank Act should protect the common people or working people who must transact their business with a bank. Just recently there was an article in some of the papers with regard to deposits. An individual wanted to deposit a large number of pennies. He went to several chartered banks, but they wanted to charge him for taking his money, which the bank could then use. Finally, the treasury branch of the Alberta government said to this man, "Bring it to us, we will take it at no charge". The treasury branch is not under the same authority as the chartered banks. Why should the banks be able to charge someone who wishes to make a desposit, whether it be in the form of a cheque, dollar bills or in pennies? There should not be a charge for making deposits. That is taking advantage of people. The Bank Act should protect not only millionaires or those who need large volumes of credit, but the common people, the ordinary, everyday people of this country, the backbone of this country. This is a matter which needs some attention.
May 6, 1980

Our banks should have as their primary purpose the service of extending credit to develop our resources. Wherever there is a situation which will benefit a community, a province or our nation, then our banks should be right in there to see what they can do to help. If that attitude were taken-it is taken by many bank managers, but unfortunately they are given orders which will not allow them to carry out what might be best for the community-it would benefit the whole nation. The bank managers know the needs of the communities they serve.
In connection with competition among foreign banks within the country, 1 would like to suggest that if foreign banks come into Canada they should provide more than just competition; we must make sure that they are coming here for the benefit of Canada and Canadians. Such banks would be expected to make a reasonable profit, but they should not be coming here to do great things for another country at the expense of the Canadian people. If the Bank Act is worded to cover this area, it will be of tremendous help.
I would like now to say a word or two about something which I am sure is mysterious to most people, and it may even be mysterious in some cases to the people within our banks. That is the expansion of credit. The government gave the right of banking to private companies and also gave them the right to expand credit under certain conditions. These banks can expand credit seven, eight, ten or even 13 times. When that credit is expanded, the money given to an industry and then returned, it is taken off the books. The loan has been repaid. Sometimes not even one dollar bill changes hands; it is all done by chequing and book entries.
I know the Canadian government has made use of this expansion of credit on a number of occasions, and properly so, although I would not say every time the government used this method it was for a purpose that I would support; but nevertheless it has been used. I would suggest that now is a good time to make sure that the banking fraternity is going to serve this country. We can do this by making sure that at least one half of the expansion of credit that takes place, because of the buoyancy in this country, is lent at a very nominal interest rate for the building of schools and hospitals.
This is not going to be in competition with anybody else and it is going to provide needed classrooms and needed beds across the country. If we could adopt a policy where only a portion of that expanded credit is used for this humanitarian benefit of building hospitals and schools at a very low interest rate, it should cut down a little on the banks' profits. Bank statements I have read do not show that they are in an impoverished condition. They can expand that credit only because they have the support of the people of this country. If there was a run on a bank and we lost confidence in our banking system, banks would go bankrupt tomorrow. Yet it is years and years since a bank has gone bankrukpt or closed its doors. I hope it is just as many years before it happens again.
I think the banks should become good corporate citizens, and, if necessary by law, a portion of the profits from expand-
Bank Act
ed credit should be used to build hospitals and schools. Low interest loans should be given to our school boards and hospital boards right across Canada. This would be a tremendous load off the shoulders of the men and women carrying the burden of the hospital and school administrations. In my view, we have a wonderful opportunity to make sure that this Bank Act is going to work for the benefit of Canada and Canadians. Let us not throw away this golden opportunity.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to address this House on Bill C-6, to amend the Bank Act. This is an act where we grant a very special privilege to a corporate group in our society, namely the banks. We are granting them the privilege to do business in our country and we are laying down the rules by which that business will be transacted until 1990. With the passage of this bill, Parliament will be allowing the existing Canadian banks to continue for another ten years pretty much as they have done in the past.
There are some exceptions. We are told that in this act we will be encouraging competition in banking, that is, unless a province decides it wants to get into the banking business. I think that is fair because the British North America Act has stated clearly that banking is the business of the federal government to legislate. We are saying in this act that subsidiaries of foreign banks may be allowed to operate in this country if the minister is satisfied that the bank in question has the potential to make a contribution to competitive banking in Canada and if we are able to provide reciprocal arrangements with the foreign banks' own governments.
I am afraid that perhaps we have not spent as much time as we should on this act regarding the competition in our banking system that we have right here at home. I refer to our trust companies and credit unions, the so-called "near banks". We submit that these are the Canadian alternative to the banking system and the only real source of competition that exists in this country today.
What has the federal government done to promote this kind of competition and improve the competitive position? In my view, the programs have not been overwhelming. For instance, the Financial Administration Act prevents the deposit of federal government funds in financial institutions other than chartered banks. The Canadian Wheat Board Act permits elevator and grain companies authorized by the board to borrow from chartered banks but not from credit unions. The Livestock and Livestock Products Act requires livestock commission agents to keep a shipper's trust account in a chartered bank, not a credit union. The Bills of Exchange Act defines a cheque as a bill of exchange drawn on a bank, again not a credit union.
When it comes to presenting government services, we note that the credit unions clear government cheques and orders at no cost. In Saskatchewan, this amounts to about 40 per cent of the clearances. In Quebec, the caisses populaires clear approximately 13 million items each year, worth about $2 billion. These figures I have quoted are 1977 figures so the volume may be increasing. Yet neither credit unions nor caisses popu-

May 6, 1980
Bank Act
laires receive compensation for their work. Granted, the banks do not charge for clearing government orders, but they at least have access to government deposits. For instance, by the end of 1978 these totalled approximately $6.7 billion. These deposits provide a considerable source of compensation for the chartered banks and, as I have already mentioned, credit unions do not have access to similar government deposits and therefore have no source of compensatory earnings.
Credit unions and caisses populaires also sell and redeem Canada Savings Bonds for the federal government which result in a net outflow of funds for which they are not compensated by federal government deposits. We say that a means ought to be found to compensate credit unions and caisses populaires for services rendered to the government. This could include balances allocated to credit unions and direct payment on a per item or lump sum basis for services rendered. I realize that not all of these impediments are created under the Bank Act; they are created under a number of other acts, but they do indicate the bias of this and previous legislation against the credit union movement in favour of banks.
In presenting the act to the House, the claim was made that we are going to be increasing competition. These claims ring a bit hollow when we look at the real promise of competition that exists here and now in the lending of money and the attendant service transactions that are not allowed to grow and develop to their full potential. This government talks about bringing into Canada foreign banks to provide competition. It almost shouts "Ignore our Canadian institutions, bring in the foreign competitors." That unfortunately is the policy which this country has been following, and we say it is about time it came to a stop. The credit unions do have a role to play here. In most western European countries, financial legislation has recognized the need for co-operative Financial intermediaries to have broad international powers similar to those accorded to the banks.
In order to serve the financial needs of the various credit union members around the world, these legislative changes have been allowed. Some examples include the DG Bank in West Germany, Rabobank in The Netherlands, GZB Bank of Austria and Credit Agricole in France which, although cooperative banks, have international investment powers in other banks.
If Parliament is going to be looking at sections of this act which provide for a Canadian Payments Association, I think it is a credible step in the right direction because it will allow credit unions to become involved more fully in the banking system of this country. The credit union movement will benefit from the proposals in the bill to create a new Canadian Payments Association through which, for the First time, nonbank financial institutions that accept chequable deposits will be permitted to participate directly in the clearing system. The credit union movement appreciates this kind of legislation because it will be in keeping with the government's stated intention to provide more equitable competition within the Canadian financial system. It will allow credit unions to have
equal access to the Canadian Payments Association in order to protect their future competitive position, especially since the CPA will become the focus for the evolution of electronic funds transfer systems that are being developed in this country.
Although the present clearing system, controlled exclusively by the chartered banks, appears to work efFiciently, there is really no indication that it is cost-effective from the point of view of the credit union system, and so they welcome the Canadian Payments Association as a clear improvement over the old system.
Direct access by near banks to the clearing system has been recommended by the Commons finance committee in its 1967 report on the Bank Act, by the Porter Royal Commission on Banking in 1964 and by the Economic Council of Canada in its 1976 study of deposit-taking institutions.
As considerable time and effort has been devoted during the past number of years to preparing for the proposed participation by credit unions in the Canadian Payments Association, we think this part of the legislation should move ahead as quickly as possible.
Parliament will be granting the privilege and responsibility of this act to the banks. It has always been Parliament that has granted charters for new banks in this country, that is, until we pass this act. After that, issuance of letters patent for any new banks will be carried out by the cabinet. I think that right should have remained with Parliament.
There are many reasons for thinking this, but I will just say that the recent history in this country of regionalized representation which we have had in the past several governments indicates that we should leave the power within the hands of Parliament. Since the impact of any of these decisions falls on the whole of the country, such decisions should rightfully be taken by representatives from all parts of the country, and this can only happen if they are taken by Parliament itself.
I do not know if the item I am going to deal with now arises from the pleas of producers of livestock that they have been ignored or whether it is a simple case of oversight. I am referring now to section 178 of the proposed act which deals with the manner in which banks' claims against processing institutions are developed. To put it simply, section 178 lays down the ground rules whereby some producers of agricultural products are protected. The section I refer to is section 178(6)(b), which gives priority to claims by growers of perishable products of agriculture that are direct products of the soil. It also gives the same kinds of rights to producers of dairy products. However, it ignores producers of livestock. Producers of livestock do not have a similar kind of protection in the event that a processing plant goes broke or bankrupt and the bank has to move in and seize the assets of that processing plant.
The problem has been dealt with quite extensively in committee. Committee hearings were conducted in 1979. The committee heard recommendations to provide for changes to
May 6, 1980

the act and it made recommendations that such changes occur. We noted in the last election that Liberals, Conservatives and this party all agreed that the change should be made. Unfortunately, it was not included in the changes made previous to the act being presented to the House. I have written a letter to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) asking him to correct this situation before we get into the committee stage so that the bill will treat all sorts of agricultural producers equitably in the event that a processing plant does have its assets taken over by a bank. It is a problem that does occur occasionally.
I will just deal with a few years. In July, 1973, City Meat and Sausage Company in Montreal went under with losses to producers. In September 1973, Coleman Packing Company went under and the producers lost money. In October, 1973, Fawcett and Cristie, in Moosomin, Saskatchewan, went under and the producers lost money. In January 21, 1975, Burkmey-ers Meat Products Limited of Burlington went under and the producers lost money. In February, 1976, the same happened to Essex Packers Limited.
Producers lost money in all of these cases because the way that the act is now written, section 88, now 178, provides that the banks get prior claim if the product that the processor is handling is a livestock or a livestock-related product. That is not the case if it is a fruit or vegetable product or a dairy product. There is a hole in the act. That should be corrected in the interests of justice and basic equity to all producers delivering products.
In order to back up this kind of producer, there are a few housekeeping things that need to be done. Instead of talking about loans to processors and manufacturers of agricultural products for the "procurement" of products, banks should grant loans for the "purchase" of products. It does not seem to be a very big distinction. What we see happening with the product, whether it is livestock or poultry moving into the plant, is that the company which owns the plant takes out a loan against that livestock without paying the farmer. If the plant does in fact go broke, then the bank collects all of the assets that are in the plant and the livestock producers are left in the lurch. That is not the case with dairy producers or fruit or vegetable producers. I am sure we will get this provision changed when we are in committee. I urge that it be corrected before the bill comes back for third reading.
As well as changing those sections of the act, we should look at releasing the amount of liability that is mentioned in the act. It has been increased. The Conservative Bill C-15 referred to a formula that would pay $64 times a particular index that was quoted. This one uses the figure of $100 times that particular index.
There are a number of problems here, and probably the solution would be just to have no limit and give the producers an unlimited amount of protection. The problem with basing it on an index is that occasionally we change the basis of the index. In 1970 we got to the point where the index of agricultural products was approaching 200, so when we got into a
Bank Act
new decade we said, "Let's turn that back to a base of 100." This could happen again in the 1980s, and because it is written into the act it would substantially reduce the amount of protection that is available to producers.
I urge the government and the House to make these small, though important, changes to the act, that we give them very real consideration, that we bring them forward in committee and that we speedily process them in order to bring about the kind of equality and justice that should exist in that section of the act.
