speakeroldname: Mr. John Evans (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my remarks to this House on April 21, 1980, in response to the Speech from the Throne, I stressed the need to view government economic policy as trying to form a stable and certain economic climate. This would be an economic climate which would stimulate growth, encourage investment and have the effect of creating new jobs.

May 6, 1980
Bank Act
This was a commitment which the government took on. When the Minister of State, Finance (Mr. Bussieres) introduced Bill C-6 for second reading, he was taking a step toward that commitment. At this time it is extremely important to the creation of a stable environment in the nation's financial sector that the Bank Act be revised and implemented as soon as possible.
Further extensions of this bill would be indeed regrettable. The current revision of the Bank Act began in September, 1974, which means that a large sector of Canada's financial community has been unable to engage in comprehensive planning for almost six years.
With the help of two parliamentary committees and as a result of the consensual reports which they submitted, we arrive at our current point, consideration of Bill C-6 at the second reading debate.
Let me make it clear that I am not asking for passage of this bill because of any deadline which may exist. I feel that this bill is the result of a careful review of what at this time would be good for Canada and good for Canadians.
[ Translation]
Our responsibility lies in strengthening and developing the Canadian financial system by promoting efficient and fair competition.

In this process we must not lose sight of Canadians who must function and live within our economic structure. If aspects of Bill C-6 will make it harder for Canadians to live within their means, it is our responsibility to redress those negative aspects. Speaking generally, I do not believe this is the case with Bill C-6.

This bill is extremely long and very complex. It lays down the framework and the basic rules within which chartered banks, the Quebec savings banks and the Montreal City and District Savings Bank were set up, operate and are controlled. [English]
There are countless issues in Bill C-6 which one can address. I want now to turn to five or six specific issues.
First, I want to consider the fact that Bill C-6 does not include a definition of the business of banking. The hon. member for Edmonton West (Mr. Lambert) raised this point in his remarks to the House, and I welcome the opportunity to ease his concern. Surely the goals of flexibility and control are the ones we should be striving for in Bill C-6. I do not see how a definition of the business of banking would help us achieve either of these goals.
It should be noted that the hon. members of the former Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs also had no definition of their own for the business of banking, although they grappled with this issue for some time.
The hon. member for Edmonton West has called for a bill with a 25-year duration, which would allow the authorities administering this bill to discharge their duties. However, since
1974 when the current revision began in earnest changes have already occurred in the Canadian economic system due both to international and domestic circumstances. Our ability to control our banking system must rest on constant review, at least every ten years, of both the charter of the banks and the regulations which have been established to control corporate development.
The government has chosen not to define the business of banking in its present review because of the evolving nature of the banking system and the obvious federal-provincial implications of any comprehensive definition. Just as today's banking institutions are quite different from those of earlier years, an attempt to define the business of banking at this point may overly restrict the evolution of the business in the future.
Ten years ago we could not have predicted the growth of the credit card system on its current scale, expanded services in the form of multi-branch facilities and flexible banking hours. Let us not limit the growth of the banking industry inadvertently by imposing long-term restrictions now.
I would further like to stress the need for competition and openness in the banking system, but at the same time these requirements depend on a structure in which to operate. That is the logic of Bill C-6, and when hon. members argue that banking will be over-regulated as a result of Bill C-6, I am confused. It seems to me that while the ground rules will be established in the Bank Act and in the proposed Canadian Payments Association Act, some details of the new banking legislation can be better dealt with in the form of regulations. This approach will provide the flexibility which is essential in a rapidly changing economy.
The number of regulations offered have been kept to a minimum. The added flexibility provided in the regulation approach and the discretionary powers given to the Minister of Finance (Mr. MacEachen) and the inspector general of banks will also enable the authorities to deal equitably with the many more participants in the system in the future.
The hon. member for Edmonton West has offered this House a critique of the regulation approach which would rest on minimal regulation, tighter definition and a longer duration of the act. I would say to him that his approach locks us into a box when our goal should be flexibility leading to financial accountability and responsibility.
The third issue I would like to address is financial leasing, and here is an area where, as I said earlier, it is important to match the intent and the practical application of the bill. The intent of Bill C-6 was to permit chartered banks to enter the business of financial leasing, defined in the regulations to ensure that bank leases were the functional equivalent of credit. The draft financial leasing regulations which were released would have permitted the banks to do leasing only through subsidiaries and the property to be leased would have to have been acquired specifically for the leasing transaction. In addition, the lease would have been on a full pay-out and non-operating basis.
May 6, 1980

The white paper noted that financial leasing was clearly a banking activity and that the participation of banks in the area would be beneficial to the financial system. It is the intention of regulations to ensure that all leases are the functional equivalent of credit and tied to specific equipment. Banks will only be able to acquire the property to lease at the request of the prospective lessee, and the banks will be disallowed from directing lessees to particular suppliers.
Specific interests, such as automobile dealers, have raised objections to allowing banks into financial leasing. Their concerns are legitimate and should be given additional consideration.
We owe a debt of thanks to our colleague, the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood (Mr. Rae), who has raised the potential conflict between the intent of the financial leasing provisions of Bill C-6 and how they would operate in practice. The information which the hon. member brought to the attention of this House was new and casts doubt, not on the principle of the financial leasing provisions of Bill C-6, but on the practical implications of this issue.
In light of the situation raised by the hon. member for Broadview-Greenwood, I believe that the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs would want to examine carefully the thrust of the financial leasing provisions of Bill C-6.
Other equally difficult issues can also be considered in committee-for example, the priority protection position demanded by the Canadian Cattlemen's Association.
Fourth, I would like to address myself to the entry of foreign banks into our economy as federally-incorporated enterprises. One could justifiably ask why foreign banks should be permitted to commence banking in Canada. Foreign banks are already engaging in business in Canada providing services which are available now from domestic banks and raising money for the purpose of borrowing in the Canadian money market.
[ Translation]
Foreign banks have intensified their activities considerably in Canada since the Bank Act was last revised. Most of those activities were handled through affiliated financial institutions set up under provincial charters. About 100 such Canadian establishments have been identified in which foreign banks have interests and which seem to deal in financial activities. Some 50 foreign banks are shareholders in those companies. About half of them are American while the others, except for seven of them, come from member countries of the European Economic Community.
In addition, there are 50 offices which act as agents for foreign banks, almost 30 of which represent Canadian bank establishments. Total assets of Canadian businesses affiliated with foreign banks and which report to the Bank of Canada now amount to over $6.4 billion.
Bank Act

At present, these foreign bank subsidiaries are not subject to the Bank Act. Foreign banks should be encouraged to set up subsidiaries under the Bank Act because of the additional competitive and innovative forces they can bring to bear in the relatively highly concentrated Canadian banking system. They are to be encouraged, too, because of the additional financial support which they, with their world-wide connections, can bring to the development of our resources, industries and trade. There is also the further consideration that if we provide a basis in law for the operation of foreign banks in Canada, we can expect our own banks to obtain reciprocal recognition in other countries which is necessary if they are to extend their participation in international markets.

The time has obviously come to give foreign banks the opportunity to do business in Canada under the terms of our federal banking legislation. The result will be greater competition on money markets and that will benefit Canadians. At the same time, the provision included in the bill will guarantee that our banking system will remain predominantly Canadian. [English]
To accommodate foreign banks in Canada, Bill C-6 has dropped the five-branch limit of foreign bank subsidiaries and has rejected the annual licensing approach suggested by some of the Canadian banks. The government has recognized that the five-branch limit suggested earlier was too restrictive on the operations of affiliates of foreign banks which might be interested in incorporation under the Bank Act.
In addition, with the authorized capital limit proposed in the new legislation, the branch limit would seem to serve no useful purpose. In this way, as the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs has pointed out, subsidiaries of foreign banks will not be restricted to locating their operations only in the largest Canadian cities.

Both committees recommended that the ceiling be abolished and the committee of the House proposed that ministerial authorization be dispensed with. Considering those recommendations and the representations received by the committees and the government, the bill embodies the recommendation of the committee of the House in eliminating the ceiling altogether. However, ministerial authorization will still be required to help in obtaining reciprocal treatment as well as some regional distribution of foreign bank subsidiaries.

I am aware that some jurisdictions prescribe annual licensing procedures for foreign banks. The Bank Act accepts the principle of licensing which will allow the government to maintain tighter control over the performance of foreign bank subsidiaries. Initial and renewed licences will be valid for a period of up to three years. It is believed that licences for three-year periods will allow adequate control over financial subsidiaries of the foreign banks.

May 6, 1980
Bank Act
Foreign banking in Canada is already a reality. It is our task to integrate foreign bank subsidiaries efficiently and adequately both to protect our domestic structure and to allow the entry of new competitive institutions.
I would now like to turn attention to the issue of competition, which has been raised a number of times in the House, and its relationship to Bill C-6. One of the major objectives of the Bank Act revision is that of maintaining and improving the competition which now exists both within the banking system and more generally throughout the Canadian financial market.
Equitable and vigorous competition within a framework of law and regulation, and subject to the basic control of the central bank, provides a number of benefits to the many consumers of financial services. Promoting competition is, of course, not the sole objective of the banking legislation and therefore in many cases provisions designed to encourage competition will also be shaped by other objectives, such as ensuring that organizations under Canadian control continue to play a dominant role in the financial sector.
A competitive environment is the most effective way of providing customers of the financial system with a wide choice of high quality services at the lowest possible costs, whether the customer be the ordinary wage earner who simply wants a convenient chequing account or a small businessman who will want a variety of payment and credit services.
The greater the degree of competition, the greater will be the degree of choice which customers will have between banks and among various types of financial institutions, the greater will be the incentive for banks and other financial institutions to offer innovative new services, and the greater will be the tendency for loan rates to be low and deposit rates to be high in relation to prevailing interest rate levels.
The bill presently before the House is the result of extensive discussions with all interested parties which began with the release of the white paper in August, 1976. Two of the major proposals in the white paper which were particularly aimed at increasing competition were as follows.
First, one group was designed to increase competition by providing easier entry of new or existing Canadian-owned institutions to the banking system. Second, a second group was designed to strengthen competition in the financial markets by constraining the business powers of banks in some areas such as data processing and underwriting of corporate securities while at the same time extending the powers of the banks to include financial leasing and factoring.
Let me now turn to outlining some of the parts of the bill which are designed to achieve these objectives, firstly with regard to promoting competition within the banking sector. In discussing the specific provisions of the bill I will divide them into two broad classes-those which promote competition within the banking system itself, and those which have an influence on either the competitive balance of the financial markets as a whole or on the interaction of the banking system with non-financial business.
As my colleague, the Minister of State for Finance, noted in his speech on second reading of Bill C-6, a number of measures are proposed to encourage an increase in the number of banks. Increasing the number of institutions offering banking services tends to widen the choice available to consumers and encourage such benefits as innovation, variety of services, and attractive borrowing and lending rates.
There are a number of provisions in the bill to encourage the establishment of new Canadian-owned banks. These facilitate both the incorporation of banks by letters patent and the conversion of an existing financial institution to a chartered bank. There are also proposals which would permit both provincial governments and non-deposit-taking Canadian financial institutions to play a role in establishing new banks.
Let me just make a few remarks on each of these in turn. As members are aware, under the existing Bank Act new banks can be established only by a special act of Parliament. This procedure applies only to chartered banks and is thus likely to be unfamiliar and to some extent a discouragement to any group of individuals contemplating the formation of a new bank. In addition, the procedure is more difficult and expensive than the letters patent route and, given the uncertainty of the parliamentary timetable, can involve risks as to timing which may be an additional negative factor in some instances.
The proposals permitting both provincial governments and existing non-deposit-taking financial institutions to play a role in establishing a new bank are intended to increase the range and types of organizations which may stimulate entry to the banking system. As the House is aware, one of the principles in the existing legislation is that Canadian banks should not be subject to domination by any particular individual shareholder or group of associated shareholders. Under the existing act, shareholdings by individuals or associated groups are in most cases limited to 10 per cent of the voting shares of a bank. At the time of the establishment of a new bank, however, entrepreneurs may be discouraged if they cannot obtain sufficient shareholdings to have an important influence on the early management of the bank and to reap an adequate return for their effort as the bank becomes a mature and successful enterprise.
The present act, therefore, permits those financial institutions which do not directly compete with the banks but which might nonetheless have some special expertise to hold up to 25 per cent of the shares of a new bank. It is also recognized that provincial governments may in some cases have a particular interest in encouraging the formation of banks with regional interests, and therefore similar provisions apply to shareholdings by provinces. These types of organizations are permitted to maintain up to 25 per cent of the voting stock of a bank for up to ten years. This provides adequate time for the bank to become firmly established, and after that period the pattern of ownership of shares must return to the 10 per cent limit which applies in most other circumstances.
May 6, 1980

It is, of course, true that when new banks are established they will inevitably be small and will take some time to grow to a size where they will be major competitors with the existing chartered banks. Therefore, the bill contains proposals to facilitate the conversion of existing financial institutions to chartered banks. This opens up the possibility that existing Canadian financial institutions with significant financial resources and an experienced staff will be able to enter the banking system and from the outset make an important contribution, and therefore further promote competition.
I might also mention that this bill provides additional flexibility in the ways in which banks may raise capital, by and large permitting them to make use of the full range of instruments available to other corporations. This will make it easier for new banks to raise the necessary capital to support rapid growth, as well as benefiting existing banks.
In addition to encouraging an increase in the number of banks under Canadian control, the bill will also permit the controlled entry into the Canadian banking industry of the subsidiaries of foreign banks, as I described earlier.
I would now like to address those aspects of this bill affecting the competition between the chartered banks sector and other financial institutions or other types of businesses, which is the second area that I mentioned earlier which has a great deal to do with the competitive thrust of Bill C-6.
In discussing the contribution which Bill C-6 makes to improving competition, it is important to note that it is competition in the financial markets as a whole rather then merely within the banking system as such which is important. For the individual consumer requiring such services as chequing accounts, savings accounts, consumer loans or mortgage loans, the competition between the individual banks is supplemented in a very important way by the operations of the credit unions, caisses populaires and trust and mortgage loan companies.
The Canadian Payments Association Act, which forms Part IV of Bill C-6, ensures that these institutions will be able to participate directly in the cheque clearing system, and equally, if not more importantly, ensures they will have a choice in the evolution of the payments system in Canada.
Since the provision of payments services provides an important first contact in attracting customers, the role which the Canadian Payments Association gives to non-bank deposit-taking institutions to participate in and influence the evolution of any new payments service will help to ensure that these organizations will continue to be in a position to provide vigorous competition to the banking system.
The government also is developing new savings bank legislation which will expand and strengthen the powers of the trust and mortgage loan companies. An important objective of this new legislation will be to ensure that trust and mortgage loan companies will have adequate and updated powers so that they may continue to play an important role in the financial markets. It should also be noted that the bill limits chartered bank mortgage holdings to 10 per cent of their Canadian dollar deposit liabilities and debentures, unless these mort-
Bank Act
gages are held in a subsidiary operating under the same rules as existing trust and mortgage loan companies. This will help to ensure more equitable competition between the banks and the specialized mortgage lenders without interfering with the significant contribution that the chartered banks now make in supplying funds to the mortgage market.
Vigorous competition in the financial markets also requires that the banks offer a full range of financial services to their customers. In some smaller centres a chartered bank may be the only type of financial institution and thus unnecessary limitations on the chartered bank powers will represent a particular inconvenience to people living in those regions. At the same time there must be concern that the banks are not given powers which would give them an unfair competitive advantage with respect to some other financial or non-financial businesses.
It is the types of considerations which I have just mentioned which have shaped the proposals in this bill affecting the business powers of the chartered banks. The banks' powers have been expanded to permit them to enter both factoring and financial leasing, as I mentioned earlier, two forms of business financing which have developed since the 1967 revision of the Bank Act and which highlights why it is necessary to have decennial reviews of this legislation. Permitting the banks to enter these markets will widen the range of choice and further competition in markets which to date have been largely dominated by foreign-controlled firms.
At the same time, legislation and regulations, particularly with respect to leasing, have been carefully designed, as I have mentioned, although we have noted that there could be some possibility for change. In particular, banks in that area are not permitted to offer non-financial services already provided by existing industries.
Other changes to the banks' powers have, by and large, resulted in stricter or more carefully designed limits on the banks' activities. One of the basic principles which has existed in the Canadian banking legislation for some time is that banks should not directly or indirectly engage in any other trade or business. This prevents a situation arising in which loan customers of a bank find that they are selling a better service in competition with their banker. Bill C-6 defines quite carefully the range of services which banks may provide and also prohibits banks, with certain limited and carefully controlled exceptions, from holding more than 10 per cent of any other Canadian corporation. For example, in the sale and distribution of securities, banks are controlled so as to avoid any potential conflicts of interest and to ensure that the securities market continues to provide a viable alternative to the banks as a means of raising funds-

speechtext:
that Bill C-201, to amend the Holidays Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, if I appear to have little enthusiasm this afternoon, it is because I have a major preoccupation, and that is the Quebec referendum. I must admit that my mood changes from day to day as I see what is happening in my chosen province. I find it an extraordinary coincidence that of the 300 or so bills on the order paper, this one should have been drawn first out of the hat and is the subject of discussion this afternoon.
Last evening, at one of the many meetings I am attending at the present time trying to present the advantages to Quebec by remaining in confederation, 1 was questioned on the ability of federal members of Parliament to do anything about changing our constitution. When we talk of renewed federalism, we talk about our faith in our country as it is presently constituted, but we cannot seem to do anything about it. This gentleman said to me, "If you want to make any change at all, you have to get the agreement of all the provinces." How true that is. He spoke of the English insensitivity.
I must admit that in the many meetings I have been attending in the last few weeks, it is abundantly apparent that we English have lots of logic which we use to try to convince our Francophone colleagues in Quebec, and on their side those who want to promote the separatist cause-the independence of the province of Quebec-that they are extremely emotional. It is very difficult to combat emotionalism, so the argument at the present time is logic versus emotion.
I made a choice. During the last war when I came to this country to train in the air force, I was stationed here in Ottawa. I liked what I saw. I enjoyed the people. I enjoyed the opportunities that were available. So, when the war ended, I decided to come to Canada and to become a Canadian. Of all the provinces in Canada, I chose Quebec. 1 did not choose Quebec because it was English. I chose it because I liked the way of life in the province of Quebec. But 1 chose it because it was one of the provinces of Canada, and my first choice was this country-surely the richest, one of the most beautiful countries in the world. We have tremendous natural resources. We have everything to make us very proud. But maybe that is our problem. We suffer sometimes from a lack of pride in our country, and particularly in Quebec I find that a lack of pride is one of the difficulties.
I have pointed out that in the province of Quebec the
provincial government already has complete and full authority
for education, culture and language-the items which are
probably the most important when we talk about the powers of the provinces-but always they bring up the point that when one is a minority one cannot always have one's own way. The problem is that everyone is a minority in some way or another. Whether it be the Francophone minority in Canada, or for that matter the Francophone minority in North America, the Francophone minority in the English provinces or the Anglophone minority in the province of Quebec, we are always in a minority position in some area and therefore we have to make compromises.
It was back in 1946 that the change I am suggesting in this bill was first proposed and the bill got as far as the Senate. Since then the bill has twice got into committee, and as late as last year it was killed in this House on third reading.
When I speak of logic, one could very easily argue that there is not much sense to bringing forward this kind of bill today because for most Canadians July 1 is presently celebrated as Canada Day. Incidentally, just last week when I was talking about this bill and the fact that it has been drawn out of the hat as the first bill, an individual said to me, "Why are you talking about making July 1 Canada Day when it already is Canada Day?" It is this kind of irritation that is causing us so much difficulty. It is an emotional thing. Obviously the people in Quebec look at it as another example of what we federal members are not able to do-to say on July 1 that we want to celebrate our national holiday using the name of our country, as every other country would surely want to do.
The secretary of state of the previous Conservative government used the words "Canada Day" in the literature from his department. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation uses the words "Canada Day". Most newspapers throughout the country use the terminology "Canada Day". The previous Liberal government on a couple of occasions-and one of our ministers who is present in the House today is well aware of this- introduced a bill to change the terminology so that we can legally use the words "Canada Day" on July 1.
I am making a plea this afternoon. I understand all the arguments of the persons opposed to this change. They are all on the record and I am sympathetic to their arguments. But it still does not change the fact that surely there should only be one designation for our national holiday.
The proposal in this bill is to simply change the wording in section 2 of the Holidays Act so that our national holiday will be celebrated on July 1 as Canada Day. I ask hon. members of this House to express their agreement with what we are trying to achieve this afternoon by passing this bill on second reading, so that once again it can continue its progress through committee and back to this House for third reading.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REPLACEMENT OF DOMINION DAY BY CANADA DAY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REPLACEMENT OF DOMINION DAY BY CANADA DAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to get up in my place and speak on this private member's bill requesting that the July 1 holiday be changed to Canada Day from Dominion Day.
May 6, 1980

I find myself, Mr. Speaker, living in a country which is not sovereign, which has a constitution that goes back over 100 years which is resident in another nation. Ever since I decided to get into politics in 1967, after living for half a dozen years in the United States, I have constantly been intrigued by the fact that this nation called Canada, celebrating Dominion Day on July 1, has a constitution resident in another country, thereby being a nation not sovereign in law or in fact. We have had to journey to our mother country to change the most basic law of this nation.
1 have attempted to review the events that occurred during our attempt to change and patriate the constitution over the last 50 years. In all instances it seemed to me that when we talked about the constitution, the first step was patriation and the second step was to seek or find the evolution of an amending formula. On that score there was not unanimity.
We then became involved in changing the distribution of powers, our institutions of Parliament and other institutions throughout the land, and always there were two sides. Some people have said, let us work on this process a step at a time. The moment we started, other people said, let us evolve a total package with a whole new constitution; let us find a process of constitutional convention, or some type of gathering, such that we can put together a whole new constitution that this nation can adopt and be sovereign in law and in fact. They have suggested we do that in such a way that the Parliament of Canada and the ten provinces can agree on this new constitution; but history has shown that this package was always too big to swallow.
Some have said we should go back to the beginning and start step by step. The moment we started for the second time some province or some party said, let us evolve an over-all concept with a whole new constitution, and the process started all over again.
This has been much like a tiger chasing its own tail around and around for 50 years or longer. 1 believe we are coming back to the same process, a process in which we will again be chasing our tail in relation to the evolution of a new constitution.
A series of events has occurred in the last 50 years during which time we have seriously tried to patriate the system or find an amending formula to revise the constitution. One of the most dramatic events that has evolved during that time is the referendum event in Quebec. That event in Quebec is not something that has cropped up quickly out of nowhere; it is something that has come up after years of consideration, after years of discrimination and difficulty in terms of self-expression by different peoples in this country.
After the Quebec referendum, irrespective of the vote, I believe that the Parliament of Canada and the provinces of this nation will have to undertake something constitutionally meaningful to indicate to the people of this country that there is a willingness, a desire and a requirement to make Canada
Holidays Act
truly a nation in every way. It is my belief that the necessary step will be patriation of the constitution.
In my estimation, and in my recognition of the law of the land and the partners in this federation, one thing this Parliament can do, with or without the approval of the provinces, is to patriate the constitution so that our constitution becomes a Canadian constitution, with Canada becoming a whole nation.
If an amending formula cannot be found during the course of patriation, then an amending formula does exist-unanimity among the provinces and the federal Parliament on changing any aspect of the most fundamental law of Canada. So there is an amending formula and that formula is unanimity. This country can patriate its constitution and become a whole nation, with an amending formula involving unanimous agreement among the provinces and the federal government on any change to the constitution.
The question has always been, is the formula too rigid; is it so rigid that the process of constitutional change becomes very difficult? One then must seek a new formula, a formula in respect of which we do not have unanimity. The Victoria charter came close to finding a formula. The Fulton-Favreau formula also came close. The provinces were unanimous then for a short period of time.
A formula that is workable can and will be found by a nation that is intent on finding a formula to amend its basic law. The point is that the first step must be taken, and the first step in my estimation will have to be taken at the earliest opportunity after the Quebec referendum. This Parliament will have to express to all the people of Canada in the strongest possible terms that it wishes the nation to become sovereign with its own "made-in-Canada" constitution, if you like.
It was my intention to speak as a member of a third group of people in this nation other than French or Anglo-Saxon. In some parts of this nation this third group of people, made up of those from countries all over the world, represents 50 per cent of the population. We have a vital interest in this nation remaining a single, whole nation called Canada.
On occasion, I have expressed a distaste for the term "ethnic" or "ethnic groups". Who are these people? I know that Canada is a nation of minorities. In national totality the French are a minority group and the Anglo-Saxons are a minority group. We are all minority groups. Canada is truly a nation of minorities. Some extra privileges have been given to some of our minorities. For example, there is language. We have adopted as our national official languages the languages of two of our major minority groups, and that is as it should be.
These two minorities acquired a pre-eminent position in Canada resulting from the great expansionary empires which in the past conquered much of the world. Interestingly, one could speculate that Spanish might have been our official language if Columbus had strayed a little farther north, and the same can be said of other explorers.

Holidays Act
Most of the remaining minority groups came to this country as refugees from turbulence, poverty, oppression, and all of them were seeking land, opportunity, freedom and eventually equality of humanism. Above all else, they sought, first, a strong nationhood and, secondly, roots.
Many came from areas of turbulence where nations crumbled and borders changed which, in turn, caused plunder, loss of human rights, human dignity, economic opportunity, broken families and loss of the privilege to hope and to dream. Most of them knew first hand the consequences of crumbling nations and passed such concerns on to their children and their children's children.

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REPLACEMENT OF DOMINION DAY BY CANADA DAY
speechtext: What of the others?

subsubtopic: SUGGESTED REPLACEMENT OF DOMINION DAY BY CANADA DAY
speechtext:
They are still to come. Most, therefore, want a strong central government and will support such a government. They know that when boundaries change minorities suffer most.
My ancestors' roots are from a part of the world where boundaries changed often and nationalism was born and died with equal ease. I therefore tremble at referenda which have implications for changing boundaries in the long term. Indeed, separation is a form of national treason. But for the freedom, the almost absolute freedom, which we enjoy in this nation called Canada, it would not be tolerated in most nations. Such is the breadth and depth of the freedom which has evolved in this nation. I therefore support the member's view of having a national day called Canada Day.
If I may be so bold as to attempt to speak for 30 per cent of the people of this nation who are neither French nor of Anglo-Saxon background, I would say that we want a strong country, strong regions and a strong federal government. Hon. members will note that I did not say a strong central government. We do not want to witness the disintegration of our country called Canada. This is our home where we have replanted our roots.
However, I can understand the burning desire of peoples of like culture and like language to congeal a nation of their own. For nationalism as the hon. member across the way has indicated, is a highly emotional matter. It is the most fundamental social instrument for perpetuating a culture, a language and a guaranteed place in history, because a nation guarantees roots and linkage with the past, as I said earlier.
In today's world, interrelated by technology and economic nationalism, there has evolved a new dimension which is called "economic well-being". Economic well-being requires access to a much larger pool of resources of technology and inter-relationship. This is provided in this modern age through something which we call a federation-federation of peoples, of areas, of groups, of governments. That is the new instrument of social organization which at the same time can provide the protection of language and culture, like ideas, like peoples, like emotions, as well as integrate the benefits of technology in such a way that the whole enjoys a much higher standard of living than each little area identified by boundaries called nationalistic boundaries or nations.
Federations can be structured and are structured. The Canadian federation is one of the oldest in the world today; I believe it is the third oldest federation. Federations can be structured in such a way that they safeguard a people's roots, language, culture, emotion and attachments. Our Canadian federation is one of the finest world examples, though it is very young. Certainly it needs revision and updating, but this is possible if we only have enough courage to make a beginning and to call our nation Canada, we have enough courage, as the hon. member across the way has indicated, to have Canada Day, a day for Canada.
Quebeckers, like the rest of us, are among the most privileged people of the world. We have land, resources, freedom, and we are progressing extensively toward equality of opportunity and humanism. It is a grand federation of co-operation, association, compromise and progress. The intent is not to homogenize cultures and languages, though at one time it was. Our roots are safe. Our future is bright. We would be committing a crime, in my estimation, against civilization itself if we allowed this federation to disintegrate or in any way break up this grand alliance of people from nations all over the world.
Why should Quebeckers try a new experiment which may be very chancy? This fuzzy and unacceptable experiment in social organization, in power politics called sovereignty-association, is a gamble of imponderable proportion for Quebeckers even if it were possible. That is my opinion. It is an egotistical, political power excursion by a few that could turn into a nightmare. It is a formula for fractionalization, a formula for constriction, a formula for human recession. It is a mirage, in my estimation a backward step.
Let no one think that new nationalistic borders will be fixed for long if this nation splits. Those new borders will be subject to constant change brought about by negotiation, coercion and even by force. Changing borders brings hardships. What can possibly be gained by national disintegration that cannot be gained within the federation?

speechtext:
I take strong exception to the insinuation from the other side that it is my intention to filibuster a bill. It is my right to speak on this matter and I do not wish to be intimidated in this fashion. I certainly do not make it a practice, and I have not made it a practice in the past when the same matter was discussed by a member on this side which was talked out on the other side of the House.
I have some constructive comments to make about this bill because I share with the hon. member, who has proposed it, a very special kind of love, a very special kind of commitment to Canada, my country, because, like him, I too came here after the great war and I too have certain expectations about this country and my future here that Canadians who are born here have never felt.
The hon. member proposes that with the referendum in Quebec now is the time for the necessary inducement and impetus to remind all Canadians that we should make a very special and public commitment to Canada in terms of naming a particular day in the year Canada Day.
As you know, sir, and as all our friends and colleagues know, it will take quite a bit more than that kind of an expression from the House of Commons to convince people in the province of Quebec that they should vote either No or Yes in the forthcoming referendum. In fact it will take quite a bit more to convince Canadians in other parts of our great country, in the west, in the north, than that kind of an expression in the House of Commons to convince them that Canada as it exists today-the status quo-is an acceptable proposition for the future.
Some of us here in the House of Commons who are not yet as fluent in the two official languages have some difficulty in understanding and in interpreting the utterances of those who call themselves leaders in this referendum debate. I, for one, do not quite understand why oui should mean no and non should mean yes. I have difficulty translating that because, when I learned my French in school, the meaning was quite ' different. Why should it be now, just because there is a referendum in Quebec and people there say they will not go for the sovereignty-association situation why will that be sufficient indication for those who live, those who enjoy and are proponents of the status quo, to sit down after 50 years and talk seriously about a new form of federalism? I do not have the faith in the people on whom we would have to rely to begin these discussions, and that if the people in Quebec vote No in the referendum, it would be the impetus required to get these discussions under way. Nor do I think the problems being debated in Quebec today are isolated to that province.
There are other Canadians in other parts of our country who are as equally concerned and who feel equally alienated and discriminated against as do people in Quebec. They are not just the people of western Canada who have legitimate concerns over the way they have been treated by confederation. There are people in the north who are suffering the hardships of frontier and remote living, without any indication from the
Holidays Act
federal government that it is determined to strive to give them a greater degree of equity and fairness. There are natives who strive to become members in the partnership of founding nations and races.
For instance, there are people of German descent-and 1 know this will sound strange to you, Mr. Speaker-who feel that they have made a contribution to the founding of this nation. They were Empire Loyalists. Indeed, one of our great provinces, the province of New Brunswick, is named after the Braunschweig regiment which fought for the honour and integrity of Canada. Many of those soldiers who were on loan to Her Majesty the Queen settled in Canada in Lunenburg and other great traditional places in Canada. These people were of German descent who fought for this great country and who had a dream and a vision about this great country. Indeed, they had the same kind of vision that I had when I came here and that my friend, the hon. member for Vaudreuil, had when he chose this country to live in and bring up his family, and to help build on the natural strength that we inherit here in Canada. These people also feel that they have a right to say something about this nation.
What is wrong with the status quo? What is wrong with the constitution? What brought on these feelings of alienation and separatism which the hon. member wants now to correct with a bill in the House of Commons which would choose one day in the year to be Canada Day? How did these things happen in the first place?
Those of us who came to this land probably made a more thorough study of history than those who were born here. For example, Sir John A. Macdonald was a federalist as convinced and convicted as is our present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). He wanted to keep everything in the centre: education, culture, and language. He wanted to regulate it all here. He was a Conservative, of course, one of the great Fathers of Confederation. But he was more of a political realist and he was a statesman who had a vision about Canada which this Prime Minister does not share. He was a realist, because he knew that Canada would never have been possible in the first place if he could not have given guarantees to the two founding nations that their culture, language and integrity would always be protected, if guarantees could not have been issued to those who joined confederation later, or to those who were initial partners, that the right over language, education and resources would always be an inalienable right and would be entrenched as such in the constitution.
The feelings of alienation and the feelings of separatism are not because of any great historic event. The feelings of separatism have come about because here we now have a new statesman who has a new vision. I respect him for it. He has one of the great minds of our time, there is no question about that. But he wants to turn the clock back 113 years and he wants to go back to the beginning.
What a great nation this would be if it would have been possible in those days to convince all the Fathers of Confederation that we should have culture, education and language under federal jurisdiction. If that had happened, there would

May 6, 1980
Holidays Act
not be ten different history courses taught in the country today. All children graduating from school would be fluently bilingual and this would have been so for the last 100 years. All children would learn just one history course. How easy it would be to stimulate a truly Canadian identity. However, that was not to be. To think that one could turn the clock back 113 years now is just playing with disaster. To think that one could bring in a bill to declare July 1 as Canada Day which would free us of all these feelings of alienation and would once again remind people to celebrate Canada as a nation, is equally naive.
As I have said, I have the same kind of love and patriotism for my country. The problem in our country is that our love has never been tested. We have never been challenged from the outside, other than in the great war when we emerged as a nation. But since then we have never been challenged from the outside, and our love for our country has never been tested.
Let there be no doubt about the one third of Canadians of whom my friend from Edmonton has spoken, who have an equally great commitment and love for our country. I will never forget the time the Prime Minister asked me to accompany a group of German Canadians who were visiting the great city of Berlin to attend an international choir festival. All of them, of course, were Canadian citizens, and all of them post-war immigrants. I will never forget the time we were boarding a ship on the Rhine River. All of us were in a cheerful mood. One got the idea, because there were two Canadian members of Parliament, one of Liberal persuasion and myself, to persuade the captain to hoist a Canadian flag. Lo and behold, when the proposition was advanced to the captain, he did indeed hoist the Canadian flag, which we presented to him.
This group of German Canadians were standing there singing "O Canada" as we were boarding the ship. Tears were streaming down their faces, so deep is their love for their country. They are new Canadians. I often wonder whether Canadians who inherited this country by birth should not take a lesson from them. I, as a new Canadian, have something to which 1 can compare this country. I can appreciate the natural advantages we have here, in a much different way.
I compare the situation to the province of Quebec. We often talk about the family home that needs rebuilding when we talk about restructuring and rebuilding the constitution. We talk about the family. I am a father with four children. If you tell one of your children all the time that the others are much better, that he cannot do it on his own and if he wants to run away from home he will starve to death, eventually he will begin to believe that.
1 wonder if our friends in the province of Quebec and our compatriots there are sick and tired of people who call themselves leaders in this referendum debate telling them that without Canada they would wither away. They have this dissent and distrust. It destroys the soul of people. I wonder if that is not the major impetus, and the people in the province of
Quebec are finally coming to their senses and saying let us find out how good we are in comparison to others.
I wonder how much we can trust those who are happy with the status quo. They have many other incentives to ensure that Quebec stays in confederation because their own political future would be in question. If Quebec votes No in this referendum, why would that be sufficient reason after all these years to sit down and have all the premiers finally come to the bargaining table, just because Quebec has said it does not want sovereignty-association? Why would that, all of a sudden, be sufficient reason to sit down and agree to a new form of federalism? I do not have the faith in the present administration in Ottawa, or indeed in any of the other statesmen who represent the provinces, that they will come together.
The Prime Minister said we should not take any steps before the referendum to confuse the issue. Even though I support the hon. member's bill wholeheartedly, I wonder whether it would confuse the issue. I do not know if the Prime Minister is right. I would have liked him to come out and say, "If you vote No, here is what we will do, and we have the agreement of the provinces to do it."
There are two things we could do, to which all the provinces would obviously agree. They have already stated that. We could patriate the constitution; bring it home. Each of the provinces at a point could designate a minister and staff to support that minister to move to Ottawa, to stay here and consult with his government on a daily or weekly basis. He would begin the process of reforming the constitution and achieving a new arrangement under confederation. Many of us have talked about this at length. It could form the nucleus of a new upper house, a house of the provinces, following the example of other countries whose constitutions are not as old as ours but are much more functional. Maybe that new arrangement could become the nucleus of a house of the provinces which has been proposed by members from both sides of the House. Let these people sit down and spend six weeks, eight weeks, one, two or five years, and not come out of the meeting room until they have something that is palatable and meets the legitimate needs and aspirations of people not just in the province of Quebec but in western Canada and the north as well.
As much as I support the hon. member on his bill, I do not think, nor would the Prime Minister think, it is the right time to approve such a measure in the House today or before May 20. It would be viewed in the province of Quebec as another candy: "Please stay in it. After all, we are going to celebrate Canada from now on and we are doing that on July 1." That is not the kind of answer the people of Quebec want. The people of Quebec want the equity and fairness to which we are all entitled as Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I have stated my position. I am very much aware of the love for Canada which exists in all parts of the country, including the province of Quebec. I am very much aware, as are all members of this House and all Canadians, that there are 18 per cent or 20 per cent in the province of Quebec who would probably wish to pursue a separatist option. The vast majority of people in the province of Quebec have a very firm and unequivocal commitment to Canada. Of course I am aware of that.
However, I am concerned when we see what is happening in the referendum debate. Why do we give so much credence to this ambiguous situation, this red herring that the premier of the province of Quebec is dragging across the floor-negotiate sovereignty association? Let us interpret this term. It confuses me. The hon. member or some of his colleagues who come from the province of Quebec are saying that if Quebeckers vote Yes in the referendum, that will be the end of Canada. I understand the premier of Quebec wants to hold another referendum, that he is merely seeking a mandate to negotiate something called sovereignty association.
Will the hon. member's colleagues who come from the province of Quebec all resign on May 21? Of course not. If the verdict is Yes, we will sit down and negotiate. Of course we will negotiate. We will have to. We will have to take the premier of the province of Quebec at his word that he will hold another referendum whether the outcome is Yes or No.
I would like my friend to answer the question: what are they going to do on May 21? Does he believe that a Yes verdict out of the province of Quebec will be the end of Canada? I do not believe that. Like him, I have great faith in our compatriots in the province of Quebec, our fellow Canadians, 80 per cent of whom would never tolerate a split up of this country.
What we have to do is see this referendum for what it is. I would have preferred a massive campaign telling Quebeckers to stay away from voting instead of participating and giving the question credence, such as we have. There are people throughout the country today who actually believe that if there is a Yes verdict, the country will split up. I do not believe that will be the case, nor do I think my hon. friend does.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a poet once said a rose by any other name would smell as sweet. Sometimes we are inclined to place too great an emphasis on a particular word. Also, I think it is wrong for any of us, at this time particularly, to be questioning the patriotism or the love of country of people anywhere in this great Dominion of Canada.
The word "Dominion" was chosen at the suggestion of Sir Leonard Tilley in the early days of our country. I think most of us admire the wisdom and the foresight of our forefathers who wrote the constitution in the first place. I admire their wisdom in not choosing a phrase such as "the Kingdom of Canada", for example, which would have indicated we were copying only one group-the British with their Kingdom of Great Britain. Sir Leonard Tilley suggested that the word "Dominion", which originally came from the French language, would mean a great deal to this country. It seems to me that the love which was envisaged by Sir Leonard Tilley and the Fathers of Confederation has, indeed, developed for the phrase "the Dominion of Canada". The suggestion was that it would tie in, too, with the strength we derive from the faith we place in an omnipotent God.
Canada is known around the world as a Christian country and we endeavour to practice that Christianity by recognizing the rights and freedom of choice of others. There exists, for instance, that splendid organization known as the Organization of Christians and Jews, in which we come together over many issues; we do not enunciate differences but, instead, we enunciate and build on areas of agreement. I believe Sir Leonard Tilley had this in mind.
Canada was founded by the British and by the French, but Canada today consists of more than the descendants of the British and French. People from countries all over the world came here. Many of them came to enjoy freedom of religion which they had not enjoyed in their own lands. The words "Dominion of Canada" indicate the importance we attach to freedom of religion, because the very words which were chosen are taken from the scripture, Psalm 72, which says, "He shall have dominion also from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth".
Hon. members should recognize that when we talk about the Dominion of Canada we indicate our faith in an omnipotent God, and those who do not wish to see this have the freedom, of course, not to do so. For myself, I look upon that choice of words as being very important; they show the faith we have in an omnipotent God in this country, freedom of religious choice, in a country whose people subscribe to many religions involving a belief in God.
A second thing which I believe Sir Leonard Tilley must have had in mind when he recommended the word "Dominion" and

May 6, 1980
Holidays Act
saw it accepted by so many people in the early days, was the great future which lay before this country because people from so many nations would come here to make Canada their home and help develop this dominion which would stretch from sea to sea.

Mr. Speaker, as I was almost concluding when five o'clock came along, I am now at the conclusion of my comments. I would like to summarize the main points I have made in the area of competition about which I was speaking.
First, it is an important objective of this proposed legislation, Bill C-6, to promote and support the vigorous competition which now exists both within the banking sector and in the financial markets as a whole. This will lead to an important benefit for both individuals and businesses, which are the customers of the banking system.
Second, there are a number of proposals in the bill which ease entry into the banking system, help support competition between banks and non-bank financial institutions, and which ensure that the competition between the banks and the nonbank sectors of the economy takes place in a fair and equitable manner.
Third, in developing the various proposals in Bill C-6 designed further to promote further competition, such other
May 6, 1980

objectives as maintaining a dominant role for Canadian controlled companies in the financial sector, ensuring the continuing soundness of the Canadian banking system and avoiding as much as possible conflicts of interest situations, have also been taken into consideration.
I would like to conclude by indicating that this particular piece of legislation has now been considered for a period of six years from the inception of its consideration in 1974. It has gone through two House committees and a Senate committee. Reports have been written. Members from both sides of the House have examined the issues very carefully and put forward their recommendations, and I think it is imperative that we come to grips with this particular issue and move this bill forward as expeditiously as possible, referring it to the finance committee, getting it back to the House for third reading, and undoing the uncertainty which now exists in the financial community with regard to when and whether this piece of legislation will be moved forward into reality for our Canadian financial institutions.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure and a privilege for me to rise this evening and take part in this debate.
I have some concerns about Bill C-6, particularly as it relates to livestock producers in the country. What was section 88 in the old act will now be section 178 in the new act. This section pertains to the problem that I think producers can find themselves facing in being unsure of whether they will be paid after the seller disposes of their animals during a marketing process.
The situation now in the country with regard to livestock producers is one of some uncertainty. Hog people are facing declining markets. I think that is well known throughout the country. This is true of cattle people to a somewhat lesser degree. We have seen falling cattle prices in the last few years, and I think some of the uncertainty producers may consider that they could possibly face during the marketing operation of their cattle could be removed by some amendments to the bill.
There are many small producers in the country. There are approximately 100,000 cattle people in the country. The average size of a cow herd is something under 100 cows, depending on the part of the country one is in. In eastern and central Canada the average cow herd probably has 60 or 70 cows. What happens to a lot of producers? They risk a fair amount of effort and energy during the year to raise cattle. They have to put up with uncertainties regarding weather, marketing conditions, and problems associated with disease. When it comes to marketing, if there is anything we can do to take away the uncertainty, it is well worth considering it. I should like to pick up something which the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor) and the hon. member for Humboldt-Lake Centre (Mr. Althouse) have said, and emphasize it relating to this aspect of the Bank Act.
Bank Act
What I am mainly concerned about is the cattle business, although the way the act reads, all livestock is in the same position. The reason I speak about cattle is that the physiological nature of the cow means that we can get only one calf from a cow in a whole year. That means that many producers could end up marketing their total year's effort in one marketing operation. A lot of value can change hands in a short period of time. It is not uncommon for a load of finished animals to bring in in excess of $20,000 to $25,000. If it happened that a producer lost this revenue as a result of inadequacies in this act, he could suffer severe hardship. I think there are some amendments we could make to this act to prevent that from happening.
I should like to see two or three changes brought about. I should like to see as much security given the producer under this act as possible so that he can have every confidence that he will be paid. To do this we need to take a look at the kind of securities that the banks take on the processors for financing the processors' operation. I also think that the level of prior claim that is in the bill, which is in the neighbourhood of $20,000 and which has been raised from $7,500 in the old act, is inadequate. In fact I think there should be no level of priority claim as it relates to producers when it comes to marketing their livestock.
The security of being paid is very important because, if you understand the marketing process, the cattle business is carried out largely on trust. Deals representing thousands of dollars are made by telephone or by a handshake. There is a lot of trust in the cattle business. The situation that we have now is such that some of the small processors could be hurt because, if a producer is looking around to find marketing alternatives or opportunities and he is trying to get the best bid he can for his cattle, the last thing about which he should be concerned is the assurance that he will be paid.
Some of the smaller packers may be in a position to bid quite favourably to obtain the livestock. If there is some concern that the producer might have about whether he is going to be paid, that could hurt small processors if they are not known by reputation or are not one of the big three in Canada, that is, Swift, Canada Packers, and Burns. Not only is it a potential problem for small producers, it is also a potential problem for the smaller processors. There are many of them in the country.
Producers take a great risk in terms of variations in the market and in terms of financing their input costs. We all know what interest rates are today. Producers have to buy fertilizer, they have to pay for fuel, for wages, for repairs to machinery, and for operating loans. By the end of that time, if there is some uncertainty associated with marketing, it is not a healthy situation. I think we could improve upon it.
I also think that livestock should be treated the same as the other commodities which are mentioned in this act. I refer specifically to the dairy industry and also to what they call the direct products of the soil. They are given prior claim and a different kind of treatment than livestock. I cannot really

May 6, 1980
Bank Act
understand why there should be this difference. I should like to quote a clause from this bill to make my point. Clause 178(6)(b), at page 187 of the bill, reads:
(i)	a grower of perishable products of agriculture that are direct products of the soil for money owing by a manufacturer to a grower for such productsis exempted. It goes on to read:
(ii)	a producer of dairy products for money owing by a manufactureris in the same category. What this means is that if I, as a producer, were to decide to move my product to a processor, that processor could not claim it as his own and use it for collateral or equity in financing his day to day operations. It means that if something then happens to the processor to whom I decided to move my product, the product is not his until I am fully paid. Also, it means that in the case of two or three days elapsing before settlement, if I were to move livestock to a packing or processing plant and if, by the time my cheque went to the bank and was cleared, the processor were put into receivership or bankruptcy, I would be put on a very long list of creditors and have to wait a considerable period of time, and would end up merely taking a certain number of cents on the dollar for my value.
What should be done and what, I hope, will be done is that recommendations will be made which would simply say that a grower of produce, or a producer of agricultural products, would be given the same kind of consideration that dairy producers or direct producers of the soil are given. It is very important that this be done. We all know that we are operating in periods of higher costs. Producers spend, in terms of the cattle business and hog business, a considerable period of production to get their product ready for market. So it is more important now than it has been in the past because of the type of dollars with which we are working.
The United States has brought about this change. In 1976 there were major bankruptcies in the United States and so the Americans brought in their Packers and Stockyard act. I should like to quote a section from that act. It reads:
A burden on and an obstruction to commerce in livestock is caused by financing arrangements under which packers encumber or give lenders security on livestock purchased in cash sales when payment is not made.
To resolve this problem, the Act states-
The act referred to here is the Packers and Stockyard act across the border.
-in effect, that all livestock purchased by a packer, and all inventories of or receivables or proceeds from meat sales, shall be held by a packer in trust for the benefit of all unpaid cash sellers until full payment has been received.
That is something that has worked very well in the United States. Since 1976 there has not been a case there of a producer having lost a cent in marketing his produce. We can observe the results very closely and try to do something similar in this country. What happens is, very simply, that every sale across the border is deemed to be a cash sale unless some other agreement is made so that cash sale, by agreement with the producer, is given some terms of sale. But unless it is deemed otherwise, the cash sale is deemed to be made. In this situation most producers feel that the product is theirs until they are paid for it, but under the law here that is not the case. The
packer having offered as security the value of goods secured but not paid for, awards to the bank the value of such goods in the case of a bankruptcy or receiving order. He does so without the knowledge or consent of the producer.
What we have here are two people thinking that they have title to the same goods and, as a result of the law being as it is, the producer is the one who comes out on the short end of the stick. The packer now has the legal right to do so. The producer believes, on the basis of morality and justice, that he has the right to expect full payment. As I said, this conviction or belief of the producer is not upheld in the law as it was previously written under section 88 nor is it upheld in clause 178 of the new bill.
I think that if packing plants are going to operate, they should finance their operations on their own equity. They should not expect the producers who sell to them to put up their equity so that the packing plants can literally finance their operations on somebody else's goods. It is tantamount to stealing, if this kind of thing is allowed to go on. You can almost make the case that if the situation is allowed to continue, we might find that some of the poorer operators would be allowed to continue in business, when really they are in the kind of condition that will put them out of business financially. They can hang on merely because they can make use of somebody else's equity. I do not believe that this should be allowed to continue.
There are three changes that I should like to see made when this bill gets to committee. We suggest that under clause 178 (6)(b) there should be a reference to a grower of products of agriculture, which would eliminate the specific reference to the dairy industry and the direct producers of the soil. That would include all agricultural products. Also under clause 178.(l)(a), to which the hon. member for Bow River referred, we should change the word "procure" to purchase. That simply means that when a processor acquires something, it is not his until he has actually purchased it and paid for it. Really that is nothing more than common sense. For the life of me I cannot understand why this has been allowed to continue in its present form without some correction before now.
I have in front of me-forgive me, colleagues-the Liberal party agricultural platform which was released from the Liberal National Campaign Headquarters on January 30. In part it reads as follows:
A change in the revision to the Bank Act (section 88) will be made in order to permit better financial security for the farmer, on agricultural produce in transit storage or processing, by providing protection to producers of all agricultural products (not just crop and dairy products) and that protection will be extended to a maximum of $250,000.
This was a campaign promise which was simply not carried out in the present act.
