subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the minister introduced this bill on May 1, as reported at page 620 of Hansard, he said the following:
-the main purpose of the bill is to strengthen and develop the Canadian financial system through the promotion of effective and equitable competition.
Then he went on a couple of paragraphs later to say the following:
The chartered banks, serving the public from over 7.450 branches, with total Canadian dollar assets at the end of 1979 in excess of $147 billion and foreign currency assets, based on their domestic and international business, of about $82 billion, are central in Canada's financial system.
We agree with the minister's contention that the banks are central to our financial and economic system, but we disagree with him completely when he implies, and in fact says very plainly, that in his view we have a banking system in which there is competition and that this act will serve to strengthen that system of competition. In our view there is no real competition in the banking business.
Probably over 90 per cent of the assets of the banks to which I have just referred belong to the big five banking companies-the Toronto-Dominion Bank, the Bank of Nova Scotia, the Bank of Montreal, the Royal Bank, and the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce. Their assets are tremendous, over $200 billion. They control by themselves, or with and through their associations with the other major corporations in this country, all the major business and industrial facets of Canadian life. In our view this bill gives the banks virtually everything they have asked for in recent years. It does so although the banks have not played the part we believe they should have played in strengthening and developing the Canadian economy.
What we have witnessed in recent years is that regional disparities are worsening, but they are accompanied by persistently high unemployment and low rates of job creation. We have the highest rate of unemployment of any of the western industrialized countries plus Japan. The deterioration of the manufacturing factor is continuing. That sector's share of the national work force was 26 per cent in 1970, and it has dropped to 19 per cent in 1979. In 1970, 21 per cent of Canada's exports were manufactured goods. Today they represent just 10 per cent. In 1970 Canada had a $3 billion deficit in manufactured goods trade, and last year it was $11.5 billion.
Foreign domination continues in most of the key sectors of our economy including petroleum, base metals, rubber, autos, chemicals, electrical products, and natural resources in general. Research and development are inadequately funded. We allocate the lowest percentage of gross national product of any of the industrialized countries of the world for scientific research and development. In the past five years $13.8 billion in dividends and interest payments left this country, and a further $8.5 billion left in management fees, patent fees,
774

May 6, 1980
Bank Act
licence fees, copyright fees and other similar payments. Our economy is potentially strong in resources, yet it is saddled with persistent and worsening weaknesses which point to the need for a large scale industrial strategy to change that imbalance and to gain control of and give direction to the economy.
What we need are efficient world-scale industries and efficient capital markets to finance the necessary technological and modernization changes. We need Canadian control over the economy to stop the drain of resources to foreign parents.
1 had the opportunity and privilege of spending a couple of days in Japan last October. We had a briefing from our ambassador to Japan during which he described the Japanese industrial strategy and approach to scientific research and development. When I got back to Canada I was able to get a copy of the summary of that program described by our ambassador. Any resemblance between the Japanese system of free enterprise and our system of free enterprise is completely coincidental. No corporation or large business in Japan would dream of expanding without consultation with and approval by the government of Japan, to determine that what was proposed was in the interest not just of the company, but in the interest of the people of Japan and of the country.
There is not the slightest possibility that a Japanese company could have done what International Nickel has done, that is, take the money it had made in Canada in profits, along with loans received from the Government of Canada, to develop mines in Guatemala and Indonesia which are in competition with their Canadian operations and which have led to a very sharp reduction in the work force with major lay-offs in Sudbury and Thompson in my own province of Manitoba. No Japanese company would have dreamed of doing that because it simply would not be permitted, yet it is done in Canada all the time.
We say there is an obvious instrument at hand, the instrument we are debating at the present time, the banking system. By virtue of the chartered banks' self-proclaimed role as the major financial intermediaries in our economy, the banks collect and distribute huge amounts of capital. Under the direction of the government these pools of capital could and should be used to promote economic development which would benefit the country as a whole, while reversing foreign domination.
We have conferred tremendous economic power on the banks because of the way the banking system has evolved in Canada, yet the banks have been left alone to develop their own distribution and investment policies, regardless of the national interest. What the government is proposing with this bill is more of the same.
Because the Government of Canada, and I am talking about the present Liberal government, that short-term Conservative government we had last year, and previous Liberal and Conservative governments, had no industrial strategy, no clearly thought out objectives and no plans to bolster the manufacturing sector, which employs a smaller and smaller percentage of the labour force, the banks are being permitted and encouraged to concentrate on making profits. I do not blame them for doing that because that is why they are in business. I blame governments for not seeing that they do the job they should be doing. They have played an important role in the mergers that have swept this country, and which, I submit, bring no real benefit to the people of Canada.
Let me just give a few examples of what I am referring to here. We have the Hudson's Bay Company gobbling up Simp-sons-Sears, only to find that they in turn were gobbled up by the Thompson interest which then proceeded to buy FP Publishers. Then we had Brascan, with the help and the financial co-operation of the Canadian Imperial Bank, moving to take over Woolworth's, a move which was unsuccessful, only to find themselves taken over by Seagram's.
The last of the illustrations I want to give tonight has reference to Dome Petroleum which has bought up in recent years Kayser Resources, Siemans Oil and Gas and a large part of TransCanada PipeLines, and this company has not paid a nickel in corporation income taxes since its incorporation because of the way in which our tax laws have been written and the way companies like Dome Petroleum can manipulate these tax laws.
Let me add just one more point about Dome Petroleum. It was the Calgary Herald, certainly no radical journal, that had a major article some months ago in which it was pointed out that for every dollar which Dome Petroleum invests in searching for oil and gas in the Beaufort Sea it gets back 97 cents from the Canadian taxpayer in the form of tax rebates. We have a system where the Canadian people pay for the search for oil and gas but the benefits go almost entirely to Dome Petroleum.
Instead of the banks being involved in fostering and helping more mergers, as they have in recent years, their investments should have gone into increasing the productive capacity of this country.
We oppose this bill because there is nothing in it that we can find which does anything to control the exorbitant profits the banks have made in recent years, and which would control the tremendous growth in the assets the banks have benefited from in those years.
Let me try to put some of the figures on the record, and I will try to be as brief as I can. Let me compare the assets and the profits of the five major banks as they were in 1973, and in 1979, six years later.
The Toronto-Dominion Bank in 1973 had assets of $9.4 billion, and by 1979 they had grown to $28.2 billion. Its profits in 1973 were $52.7 million, and in 1979 they had increased to $160.4 million.
The Bank of Nova Scotia in 1973 had assets of $10.3 billion, and by 1979 they had grown to $34.8 billion. Its profits in 1973 were $56.8 million, which had grown in 1979 to $180.9 million.
May 6, 1980

The Bank of Montreal has assets in 1973 of $14.4 billions, and by 1979 they had grown to $38.1 billion. Its profits were $68.5 million in 1973 and they were $228.7 million in 1979.
The Royal Bank had assets in 1973 of $18.3 billion, and by 1979 they had grown to about $57 billion. It had profits in 1973 of $99.2 million, and by 1979 these had grown to $270.7 million.
The Canadian Imperial Bank had assets of $16.1 billion in 1973, which had grown to $45,995 billion in 1979. Their profits went from $92.9 million in 1973 to over $201 million in 1979.
Let me summarize those figures. The increase in assets in those six years from 1973 to 1979 was over 300 per cent, and the increase in profits was over 250 per cent. Let me put just one more figure on the record. In 1975, the year in which the present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Liberal government felt that our inflation had reached crisis proportions, to combat inflation the government brought in the wage and price control program, and profits increased over 1974 by 46 per cent. It is the banks which should have had their profits controlled rather than the workers having their wages controlled.
We believe that the profits of the banks should be controlled and that they can be controlled by the government-because it controls the interest rates-by the interest rate spreads and by surtaxes on bank profits.
We are opposed to this act for another reason. This act would permit and indeed encourage bank directors to hold other business directorships. We believe that that is bad for this country, and we are not alone in this belief. As respected an organization as the New York Times said several months ago about Canada's policy of permitting bank directors to participate in interlocking directorships:
The concentration of banks is so great-
And they are talking about Canadian banks.
-and the alliances of companies with specific banks so strong that a single bank can find itself financing both the suitor and the sought. Such was the case last fall for the Bank of Commerce when Brascan went after Woolworth's.
The Times went on to say:
The banks with their corps of 60 or 70 directors each and their circling clans of corporations also provide the detailed intelligence system so vital in the fraternity that is Canada's business establishment. This, and a system of interlocking directorates, provide the tips, the data, the shared experiences and, above all, the connections that smooth Canada's merger movement. It is no coincidence, for instance, that Consumers Gas and Hiram Walker, both use Toronto-Dominion, where Hiram's chairman, H. Clifford Hatch, is a director.
Many in this network grew up at the same elite schools together, such as Upper Canada College. They join the same clubs, such as the Toronto, Ontario or Albany Clubs. Their children marry within the network.
That is not my view, although I subscribe to it. That is the view of as important and serious an organization as the New York Times.
We did a little work to see how this system of interlocking directorates really works in this free enterprise system of ours. I would like to put on the record a few illustrations.
Let me begin with the Bank of Nova Scotia. The chairman is Cedric E. Ritchie, who is also the president and chief

executive officer. Among his other directorships, and I will not list all of them because it would take too long, are Empire Realty Company-there is the real estate industry; The Canada Life Assurance Company-there is the insurance industry; and Olympic Trust of Canada. George C. Hitchman is deputy chairman, and among other companies is director of Algoma Central Railway. So, the railways are represented. E. J. Courtois is vice-president and director of Gaz Metropolitan, which takes care of the gas distribution system in Quebec, Trizec Corporation-the giant real estate developers-Brinco Limited, Norcen Energy Resources Limited and Phoenix Steel, to mention a few. The hon. John B. Aird-and I am sure that my friend, the hon. member for Nepean-Carleton (Mr. Baker) will remember Mr. Aird when he was a Senator and chief fund raiser for the Liberal party-is not just a director of the Bank of Nova Scotia, but is also a director of Algoma Central Railway, Consolidated-Bathurst, Domglas Incorporated, National Life Assurance Company; and I could go on and on.
Let us look at the Toronto-Dominion Bank and the chairman and chief executive officer, Richard M. Thomson. Mr. Thomson is also director of Cadillac Fairview Corporation- another giant in the construction industry; Canadian Gypsum Company, Eaton's of Canada, the Prudential Insurance Company, Texasgulf Incorporated. J. Allan Boyle, president of the Toronto-Dominion Bank, is also a director of Regtor Investments Limited, Excelsior Life Insurance Company, and Aetna Casualty Company.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is indeed a pleasure for me to rise and speak on Bill C-6. In my opinion it is time that the Bank Act was improved and changed. Many of the revisions that are presently included in the bill before the House have been before this House of Commons for a good number of years, as was pointed out previously by another speaker.
It is time for improvement, despite the fact that the banking system in this country is probably the very foundation of our free enterprise system, a system that has worked immeasurably well not only for Canada but for all nations in the free world. It is one that I think should be continued under that particular set of rules.
I listened with interest to some of my NDP colleagues, and although it was not included in the last speaker's speech, there have been suggestions that perhaps we should be looking at the possible nationalization of banks in Canada.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: The Tories want to nationalize the banks?

speechtext:
I would strongly criticize that particular position if indeed it is the policy of the NDP. It is very, very difficult to try to determine what NDP policy is this day. As a matter of fact that party was instrumental in introducing a motion into this House which brought about the downfall of an extremely responsible government last December. The members of the NDP are sitting here on this side of the House as though they were the epitome of righteousness, condemning the very government they put in place and helped to support during the early years of the 1970s. We would see this situation again, I am sure, if the same set of circumstances were in vogue. It has been well said by a colleague that lack of principle is quite obvious.
During this time of repression, I look with interest at the great nationalization nation. 1 suppose the great champion of the nationalizing nations of the world is Sweden. Sweden has recently been in the news and we can now see the nationalization of its industries, including financial institutions, which was supposed to be such a workable situation among businesses, banks and unions and things of this nature that make it all happen, make the economy go around, and create jobs, seems to have fallen apart at the seams. The same thing very nearly happened in Great Britain. Fortunately for Great Britain and the people there, a Conservative government was elected last year or the year before. They are now in the
Bank Act
process of salvaging what little bit was left after a decade or more of a socialist-labour government, the counterparts of the Canadian NDP.
As was stated by a former speaker, apparently the NDP approach to the solutions of the country's ills is to lower the interest rates. This seems to be the whole thrust of their position, lower the interest rates, get the interest rates down at all costs. It does not matter that it will deter the investment of foreign capital in this country, that foreign investors would obviously not be interested in coming to this country with their investment money which this country of 22 million or 23 million people dearly requires.

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext: What is your policy?

subtopic: BANKS AND BANKING LAW REVISION ACT, 1980 MEASURE RESPECTING BANKING INSTITUTIONS
speechtext:
The policy of this party when we were in power was to encourage foreign investment for the benefit of Canadians so that the net result would be a better way of life and better standard of living for Canadians. It is unfortunate that that policy did not have an opportunity to be implemented and put into place.
The other interesting aspect of lower interest rates and all of the goodies bundled up into the NDP package seems to be that, if there is not enough money to go around, we will crank up the old printing machine, grind out more dollar bills, hang them on the line, and hopefully we will not need them until such time as they have had an opportunity to dry on the line, and with those dollars we will purchase all of the goodies and provide all of the jobs that we so desperately need in this country.
What they conveniently neglect to address themselves to is what happens to all of the goods and services that are not presently available in Canada because our manufacturing service is not currently manufacturing all the necessities of life that Canadians need in order to enjoy the lifestyles that they have become accustomed to enjoying.
What about the cost of lettuce during the winter months as it comes to us from California, and all the other imported foodstuffs that come into this country? How do we afford them? I know the answer. Just speed up the old printing machine, crank out more dollars, put more dollars in the pockets of the people. It does not matter that they are worthless.
Canada is a marvellous country with probably the greatest future, provided we don't blow it with such frivolous policies as the NDP might force upon us. I suppose one of the suggestions, if everything else is to be nationalized, is that the unions should be nationalized as well and brought under the control of government. I have never heard anyone from that party address themselves to that, but I suspect that would just naturally flow. Unions would become part of the nationalized process as well. Perhaps at some other time we could have some comment on that situation from the NDP.
Last year the net debt of this country was billions of dollars. It is a debt we certainly cannot afford. We have lost more

Bank Act
man-hours in this country through strikes than any other nation in the world, and the loss to the economy of these dollars is just fantastic. I am very concerned that the irresponsible attitude of the present government, backed up by its cohorts on this side to my left, is contributing not only to labour unrest but to the fact that our production is among the worst in the world of the industrialized nations. It is great fun, and I suppose it makes great political games for the socialists to take on the hustings when the time comes, but this is a very serious business and very serious situation.
1 point that out because I feel that nationalization is not the solution to this country's ills. I believe that the banks in this country have proved to be an immeasurable success with their contributions to this country, and to the very foundations that have made this nation great, and made all free nations of the world great under the free enterprise system. Obviously the banks of this country know their business. They know it very well.
As has been pointed out, the banks are extremely successful. They are successful in the business they are in, the money business. Their profits are more than respectable; in fact, they are questionable. There is no question about it. When profits exceed those amounts that can be rationalized by any thinking person in this country, then we must take a look at the way those dollars are made and at whose expense.
How do they do as well as they do? One reason is not by being a bunch of nice guys. The banking institutions of this country have formulated a policy over the years of obtaining collateral that, quite frequently has to be at least equal to and in a good many instances surpasses that of the particular loan or whatever that company or individual might want to have from them. Of course one of the reasons they have been able to do this is because they have had a corner on the money market of this nation for so long.
We have had relatively few banking institutions in this country as banks are known to most individuals. It is a healthy sign that we, as a nation, are prepared to look at and accept that there is room for competition in the banking industry. As was pointed out by the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Taylor), the important aspect of competition in the banking industry is that the profits coming into the country through the medium of a bank if it is foreign controlled, are reinvested in Canadian businesses or businesses that are going to accrue major benefits to the Canadian people and the Canadian nation.
The attitude of banks over a period of years on a good many occasions and in a good many instances has been ruthless. They have had an opportunity to charge service charges when profits were in a very excessive position. The inclusion of new banks where profits are going to be reinvested in Canada will be of benefit to the nation.
Banks should stay in the business that they know. I am disappointed that this bill does not deal with that. In fact it seems purposely to exclude it. One of the most important provisions in the new Bank Act that has caused concern is the section that will permit the banks to enter into the auto leasing

field, presumably in competition with auto dealers and others now involved. On the face of it one might consider that competition of this kind can have obvious benefits. I doubt if this would be the case.
I have discussed this matter with my hon. friend from Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) and others, and he and I, along with a good many others in the House, have concluded that the public might not benefit if auto dealers, the heart of the business community in many cities and towns, particularly in the rural areas, are jeopardized by unfair competition. So we have to ask: when is competition unfair? Mr. Speaker, it is unfair when the rules are changed without giving all those in the field equal opportunity. The banks already receive many benefits and have no responsibility in the auto business in terms of keeping facilities open. If we change the rules we must be careful of the result. If the result is to bankrupt auto dealerships, the public gains nothing.
The auto industry is presently passing through a particularly strenuous period. Every day we read in the newspaper about auto plants shutting down, the difficulties which Chrysler is experiencing, and the decline in sales. Many dealerships are making only a marginal profit, and some are making no profit at all. Their position, in relation to that of the banks, is very serious. It is my opinion, and the opinion of a great many members of this House, that the public would be much better served if the business of auto leasing were left in the hands of those who understand this business best. It should be left in the hands of those who obviously have the facilities to conduct it; the dealers have the repair shops and, more important still, they have a close interest because automobiles are their primary source of income. I would urge the minister to re-evaluate his position on the question of the banks entering the leasing field and to introduce provisions which would protect a vital and important section of business in Canada.
I should like to deal, as well, with the subject of credit cards and banking institutions-the buy now and pay later plans to which we are so often exposed in this country. I suggest it is not always in the best interests of the public when loans which likely command an extremely high rate of interest are not only available to the public but are promoted. We have all seen the signs in the windows of the banking institutions-"Come to the land of fun and sun," showing mama and papa and what-not basking in the sunlight on some tropical island. The message is, "Don't worry about the cost because you can go now and pay some time in the future when you get round to thinking about it." Mr. Speaker, we know this is not reality; this is not the way things are. This is a cold-hearted world, though people are somewhat prone to forget it. I do not think it is healthy for this nation to be bombarded with advertising of that type and to become a nation of debtors because banks and other financial institutions are determined to increase their profits at the expense of people who might be carried away by an urge to do someting they can ill afford.

I would ask the minister to consider some type of regulation which would deal with this type of promotion promising a life in the sun, a never-never land with no need to worry about paying for it. Attention has already been directed to the difficulties in which producers find themselves when stock and carcasses become the property of the processors, under the Bank Act, before they have actually been paid for.
I suppose there is no single group of individuals in this country who have to work harder than the farmers, or who experience more difficulty in making ends meet. I agree this is an unusual situation, but I believe we should show some compassion toward these people whose work is so vital to the nation, by dispensing with the provision in the bill which places them in the same class as International Harvester or any other of the equipment companies and suppliers in the eventuality of a processor going bankrupt. There is one other item in the bill which I Find somewhat distressing. It seems that Parliament is to lose the right to grant charters to banks. I suggest this is an erosion of the rights of Parliament. Heaven knows, under the present government, in the last ten years there has been a great deal of erosion of the rights of Parliament, and I question the motives of the administration in including such a provision in the act. As I understand it, we will no longer have the right to debate in this House the issuance of new banking charters in this country. The authority is to be given to cabinet or some extension of the government, and these charters will not be brought before the House for debate.
I do not believe this is a healthy situation. I do not believe it is healthy for the future of the country to have this continuing erosion, because of a government that is now well known to be arrogant in a good many of its directions and decisions. Speaking about growth in bank assets, I think it is wise that we get it into perspective in two senses. First, I have indicated that, if anything, the Canadian chartered banks are actually losing ground in the world banking community as far as size is concerned. However, second, I suggest that the mere fact that the banks have grown at such a rapid rate should be one of the reasons our socialist cousins should be standing up in this House and saying, "Let us get on with the passage of Bill C-6 so that we can in turn bring the foreign banks under at least some type of control or regulation as contemplated in Bill C-6".
Here are the facts: In 1968, which was the year after the present Bank Act was passed, total bank assets in Canada were $36.7 billion. At the end of last year they had reached $225 billion. Of that amount, in 1968, about 21 per cent of their assets were made up in the form of currency. Today it is approximately 36 per cent. I think it is healthy that we have institutions which have got out into the world market and have been able to increase their assets in that market to the extent I have indicated. So we should be encouraging, not discouraging, those banking institutions in their endeavours to be, 1 suggest, world-scale industrial companies, or banks in this case, of which, as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) said, we needed more.
The reason I will suggest tonight to hon. members that we get on with passing Bill C-6 is that it behooves this House to recognize that the Bank Act is one of the few sunset types of legislation that we have in existence in Canada. It is a good concept, the concept that you pass a bill for a limited term, that you can review it, amend it, and then repass it, presumably with improvements. Initially it was intended that the Bank Act should be passed every ten years after a suitable review in committee and in this Parliament. That review has taken place. There have been prolonged debates with respect to the revision of the Bank Act.
Let me review what has happened since 1975. In that year the Department of Finance asked interested parties to submit briefs, in time, they said, for the preparation of the 1977 revision of the Bank Act. In August of 1976 a white paper was published in which the general principles to be incorporated in

the new Bank Act were set out. By the fall of 1976, the Senate banking committee requested and received a special reference to study that white paper. The House requested the same reference but the government refused to pass a motion in agreement because opposition members were not agreeable to limiting the House debate on this issue. That was in the fall of 1976.
In June of 1977 the Senate issued its report for government study. The government again requested submissions from interested parties. Some delay was caused by provincial objections that membership in the Canadian Payments Association required holding reserves with the Bank of Canada, that is, the near banks which, under the jurisdiction of the provinces, would have to hold reserves with the Bank of Canada. The provincial objections became quite loud as they felt that somehow their responsibility for near banks was being jeopardized.
The government of the day then decided to rethink those proposals and came to an understanding with the provinces. Meanwhile, the old bill, that is, the present Bank Act, which would have been extended to June, 1978, was extended once again. The opposition was anxious that a new bill be introduced, yet the government said it needed more time to study the recommendations. By May 18, 1978, we had introduced Bill C-57 which contained most of the broad proposals set out in the white paper but made a major departure from the white paper on the issue of the reserve requirements of the near banks. In June of 1978 the session ended and the bill died on the order paper. On November 2, Bill C-15 was re-introduced, which was substantially in the same form as Bill C-57, and after a very brief House debate it was referred to the finance committee of the House. Mr. Speaker, the point I am making is that again we have an example of our socialist cousins, as my friend, the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre likes to be referred to, liking to have the best of both worlds, in that while they sat through those committee hearings they accepted substantially all the recommendations and the points that were raised, but now they like to pretend that they are divorced from what went on before and they can stand up on behalf of whoever they stand up for and damn the bill, as they did tonight.
What I am suggesting is that I think the time has come, bearing in mind the long history of this legislation and the committee's reviews, for us to get on with passing Bill C-6. Certainly there are certain points which I hope will be raised in committee and there might be amendments yet to be made to this bill, but I believe it is substantially in a form that is acceptable, in a form that the people of Canada would like to see it passed and, above all, it is in the form that the financial community of the country, the industrial community and the banking community, would like to see it passed to bring some certainty back into this world instead of the uncertainty with which we have been living.
I brought us up to 1978. You will recall that when we formed the government in this country we acted promptly with respect to the bank legislation. We reviewed the reports of both the Senate committee and the House of Commons committee on the Bank Act, and in the fall of last year we introduced Bill C-14, which is substantially the bill we now have before us, namely, Bill C-6. Surely there is no disagreement in substance with regard to the provisions of Bill C-6 either from our side, from the government's side or, I suggest, from the socialists to my left. So why the prolonged debate?
If what we are witnessing is a general frustration that we were robbed of a proper budgetary debate by the Minister of Finance, whom I see in the House at present, if we are sensing in the House a degree of frustration because the theft was made, then let us do what we can to bring the Minister of Finance to account.
For example, I think it was quite proper in a committee of the House today to suggest that the interest rate review that we had instigated while we were in government be continued in a committee of the House. Frankly, I think all members of the Opposition, including the socialist members on that committee, were most startled to see that, to a man, the government members on that committee used their heavy-handed majority to vote down the mere suggestion that a committee of the House should review the interest rate structure and what could be done to achieve lower interest rates in this country, or at least to relieve the people from some of the side effects of our high interest rates.
What I am trying to point out is that surely Parliament is not functioning properly when we have before us a bill such as Bill C-6 which has been debated, or at least reviewed, since 1975. When we have a bill that is substantially agreed to on all

May 6, 1980
Bank Act
sides of the House, surely we are not operating properly by having a prolonged debate on that bill and, at the same time, having government members virtually stalling a meaningful review by a committee of this House of interest rates in this country. Having said that, and having urged that members get on with the passage of this bill, I should like to go further and say what are some of the pluses in the legislation.
I know the foreign bank question perhaps has been one of the more controversial, contentious issues which has been raised during the debate over the years concerning the Bank Act revisions. But I would suggest that if we are properly going to come into the 1980s, it is time we accepted that there is more to be gained than to be lost in Canada by making us an international banking centre, and that is exactly what the admission of foreign banks to a greater extent into Canada will do for us. I think there are pluses to opening up the banking system in Canada and letting, under the regulations that are contemplated in the act and in the regulations, foreign bank activity grow in Canada.
Since 1967 when the present Bank Act was last revised, foreign ownership of any chartered bank in Canada, as we know, has been restricted to a maximum of 25 per cent. However, there were no restrictions placed in that act on the establishment of subsidiaries by foreign banks. Since 1967 numerous foreign bank subsidiaries and representative offices have been established in Canada. For example, in the office building in which I had my office at one time, one day I counted 26 foreign bank agencies or representative offices alone. How ludicrous it is for us to allow that situation to continue, and perhaps most important, think how we look in the eyes of the world.
At last count there are supposed to be 100 corporations doing business in Canada that, to all intents and purposes, are really in the banking business and are controlled or owned in some instances by foreign banks. About 50 foreign banks have an equity interest in these corporations according to the Department of Finance press release of May, 1980, which I know my friend, the Minister of Finance, probably wrote with his own hand.
In addition to the 50 foreign bank representative offices, there are about 30 representative banks which do not appear to have any investments in Canadian financial corporations. The total assets of Canadian affiliates of foreign banks reporting to the Bank of Canada currently exceed $6.5 billion. In short, in addition to the banking assets to which I have referred, we have a situation where there is over $6 billion of banking activity going on within the affiliates, the agencies and the representative offices of foreign banking concerns in Canada. This act will attempt to regulate to some extent that activity, and I think that is good. First, I think it is good that hopefully we will know better what those banking concerns are doing, and second, it will help our banks expand into the foreign markets that we need so badly.
Also I suggest that as we face the current account deficit that we do in this country-the worst of any western industrialized nation-it is important that we recognize that to the degree we become more of an international banking company it should help our trade activity in those foreign countries. In short, let us be less inward looking, let us be less insular, let us be more world-minded, so that we can tap some of the tremendous economic activity that is churning in the world and which could churn to our greater advantage if we accepted the reality of the world such as it is today. I would suggest that among the various reasons we could give for endorsing the concept of opening up our system to foreign banks is the need to increase competition in Canada.
As we have indicated, we have large banks. On a world basis the largest is about thirty-fourth, but in terms of Canada they are undoubtedly very large. Surely it behooves us to open up the system to allow some of the foreign concerns to lend their innovative ways, their new approaches, their new techniques and their ingenuity to our Canadian banking system. I would suggest, from people who have talked to me, that already the foreign banks in the limited extent that they have been active in the country have rejuvenated many aspects of our banking business, and I think that is to be encouraged.
One point which I think was raised very effectively at committee was that, if we do not open up our banking system, we will find that there will be less reciprocity open to us as Canadians when we try to go into foreign banking markets ourselves. In short, let us catch up to the 1980s. I feel that if the socialist rump group to my left-

subtopic: METRICATION-REQUEST METRIC COMMISSIONERS BE RELIEVED OF DUTIES
METRICATION-REQUEST METRIC COMMISSIONERS BE RELIEVED OF DUTIES
speechtext:
I wish to thank you, Mr. Speaker, for according me the privilege of bringing to your attention a very important matter. I wish to place before this House some facts about the metric conversion program in this country. They are facts, not arguments.
The fact is that the Liberal government has created a monster in the most devious fashion possible. The metric system was thrust upon the Canadian people by an order in council and by regulation. Surely it must rate as the number one subject which rankles Canadians. It is a costly mistake. It is too much, too soon. It is an over kill.
The metric conversion program was first introduced to this House in the form of a white paper which was tabled in 1970. The government had the courtesy at the time to give our spokesman, Mr. Ged Baldwin of Peace River, advance notice, but even then he had only scant minutes to reply in the House to a subject which has had, and is having, sweeping ramifications across this land. Even then Mr. Baldwin warned the government of the day of the pitfalls of proceeding with haste with metrication unilaterally, without working in concert with the United States, the country with which more than two thirds of our trade takes place.
No, the government decided to operate by stealth. Metrication was introduced through the back door and, like Topsy, it just grew. Last week in the House the Minister of State for Small Businesses (Mr. Lapointe) conceded that no formal metric bill had ever come before this House. I question, since this is the case, whether the metric program has effect in law. It was not passed by this House. Were indeed the estimates for the program passed by this House? I think not. What is the legal glue which holds this sticky wicket together?
We have had occasion to amend existing pieces of legislation so that they conform with the SI scale of measurements, amendments which could allow the use of metric standards in lieu of the inch-pound measurements. I would like to lay some facts before you, Mr. Speaker. Fact one, the metric program was introduced to the House in the form of a white paper. Fact, the white paper was not debated, merely commented upon by opposition spokesmen, and very briefly. Fact, opposition spokesmen warned the government of the suicidal course of going it alone without parallel measures coinciding in the United States.
Fact, the metric commission was established by executive order or by cabinet. Parliament was bypassed in the creation
May 6, 1980

of the overseers of the metric program. Not even the NDP raised a word about this fact. Fact, as the Minister of State for Small Businesses has readily admitted in his reply to my question of privilege, an omnibus bill which would allow us to debate the principle of the metric system was never brought before this assembly.
Fact, the metric program was imposed on the good citizens of three major centres of population, Peterborough, Ontario; Kamloops, British Columbia; and Sherbrooke, Quebec. Fact, the program has not been well received and the government has had to pull in its horns in all three areas. Fact, in Peterborough, Ontario, residents boycotted city stores which had to use metric and did their shopping in the neighbouring communities, which was a severe financial hardship on Peterborough merchants. Fact, despite the unpopularity of the metric program, the bureaucrats intend to introduce metric, cold turkey, in 25 or 26 other cities and towns early next year.
This is folly, Mr. Speaker. Why is the government so prone to rush in when it is so obvious there is built-in resistance to an unpopular program? Why can the government not admit a mistake and draw back until the time has come for metric? It may not be in my lifetime, but perhaps sometime in the distant future. Our young generations, our school children, will have little trouble assimilating metric along with their other studies. Perhaps the solution to the dilemma would be to have school children study both systems, become conversant with both, in order to plan for that day when metric might be introduced in a sane and rational fashion when it is needed.
You cannot teach an old dog new tricks, Mr. Speaker. I, for one, will probably always rely on the old measurements. Even though metric has been in effect for some years, I still convert in my head metric to the old scale.
I implore the government not to proceed with this foolhardy course it is taking. If it persists, let us get it out into the open, get a bill before Parliament where the principle of metric and metric conversion can be intelligently debated. Let us get it out in the open so that the elected representatives can voice the concerns that are being expressed to them by angry and confused constituents, businessmen and ordinary citizens.
If, as the Minister of State for Small Businesses admits, a metric bill has never been debated in this House, now may be the time to do it, now before the bureaucrats ram the program down the throats of Canadians in 25 or 26 other centres. Let us have a free vote.
Let us work in concert with our neighbour to the south. Let us find out what its plans are vis-a-vis the metric system. Let us get off this unilateral, undemocratic course, pushed at us by an arrogant government. The Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said he would listen to the petitions of western members; let him now fulfil that promise.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph Ferguson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State, Small Businesses):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Small Businesses and Tourism)
subtopic: METRICATION-REQUEST METRIC COMMISSIONERS BE RELIEVED OF DUTIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps I
Adjournment Debate
should quote the president of the nation to the south, Mr. Carter, who, in January 1980, said this:
1 personally support and encourage the use of the international metric system of measurement in the United States. Conversion to the metric system will help us to expand America's export market.
Mr. Carter concluded with these words:
Because I believe metric conversion holds important long-term benefits for our country, I am taking steps to encourage the use of this system in the private sector as well as in government.
With regard to the comment on working in concert with the United States, it is interesting to note that plans for the automobile industry in north America are for it to be completely metric by 1982.
Legislation on the subject of metric conversion has had considerable debate in this House. The use of the metric system was made legal by Parliament with the passage of the metric Weights and Measures Act many years ago. The Weights and Measures Act of 1971 included an amendment which made the international system of units the legal embodiment of the metric system in Canada. The policy that metric conversion was inevitable and in the national interest was established with the House leaders of all parties on January 15, 1970, speaking in the House in support of the white paper on metric conversion in Canada.
The Consumer Packaging and Labelling Act of 1971 made it mandatory for all pre-packaged goods to carry a metric contents declaration.
The Statute Law Amendment Act of 1976, which was debated in this House over a period of nine months, gave the governor in council the power to set dates in any sector of the economy after which the use of the customary or imperial system would be illegal.
A program of guideline dates for metric conversion recommended by Metric Commission Canada after consulting with industry, labour and consumer groups, was approved by the government and debated in the House of Commons on March 17, 1975. The Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs studied this matter at length and voted unanimously in favour of it. It reported it back to the House of Commons on December 17, 1976, with a recommendation that the House consider the advisability of adopting this program and also introduce additional legislation to metric conversion. Subsequently the Statute Law Amendment Act of 1976, was passed by the House of Commons on July 25, 1977, and received royal assent on August 5, 1977.
In view of the fact that metric conversion currently is proceeding or has been completed in 88 of the 100 odd sectors of the economy which have published conversion plans, with the phasing and co-ordination of Metric Commission Canada, there is a proven continuing need for the commission staff and the commissioners to ensure that orderly conversion is made to the best advantage to consumers and to Canada.
It is interesting to note that an industry in my constituency has expanded its production threefold since going metric because it can now export to Europe.

May 6, 1980
Adjournment Debate

subtopic: TRANSPORT-MOVEMENT OF GRAIN-ALLOCATION OF HOPPER CARS TO BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY
TRANSPORT-MOVEMENT OF GRAIN-ALLOCATION OF HOPPER CARS TO BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to debate a matter which I discussed briefly during the question period with the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pepin). I choose this timing because it is my understanding that the minister visited this strange and mysterious land beyond the rocks which is called Colombie-Britannique. He just returned from there. I presume he had some discussions with the politicians and transport managers there. Maybe, just maybe, his parliamentary secretary will be able to make an announcement tonight with respect to this matter which has been of concern to me and the people I represent in the farm community in the Peace River area.
I asked the minister in the House why it is that the British Columbia Railway, which is known to some people in his department as a foreign railway because there is no direct subsidy or involvement by the federal government or the national railways in the ownership and operation of that railway, has never been allocated any hopper cars. These are the cars, as hon. members know, that are part of our modern grain delivery system. They are now essential to fulfilling the task of getting our grain to market.
The reason the minister used for not allocating any hopper cars to the railway relates back to the Crowsnest freight rate. As hon. members know, it has always been the understanding that the railways would have to haul grain from the prairies to the ports on a subsidized basis because, without that, it would be very difficult to compete in world markets. It has always been the understanding as well that, in return, the railways were granted large areas of land and other concessions. Over the years they have been granted other subsidies like branch line subsidies and so on. All of these things were never granted to the BCR.
The minister argues, and he said to me in answer to my question in the House that the subject is debatable. That is what I am doing here. He said the BCR, because all their grain goes to the west coast from the Peace River country, is not obliged to haul its grain on the same terms and conditions that the national railways haul through the Crowsnest Pass. That is quite true. However, nobody would ship any grain on the BCR if it were not shipped and transported in competition with the rates that prevail in other parts of the western prairies. The Peace River country, knowing the geography of this country, is the last part or the tail end of the prairies.
When the BCR extended its line to Fort St. John in the B.C. portion of the Peace River country, it had to compete with the Crowsnest rates. It began in 1958 to haul grain at the same price it was hauled to other ports by other railways. Therefore, that argument does not hold true. It has been very disconcerting to us because many farmers in the Peace River country have not been able to fill their quotas. There were never any cars. There are not sufficient cars there now to move the grain from the elevators to the port.
As well, the system is being modernized and changed to the point where these cars are essential because it is very difficult to unload the conventional cars at the ports now with all these modern elevators.
In 1973 the federal government purchased the first 2,000 hopper cars and allocated them to the national railways. They were allocated in proportion to the volume that these railways were hauling, CP and CN. CP got 52 per cent of the initial order and CN got the rest. They passed them on to the other railways such as the Northern Alberta Railway which competes with the BCR to some extent for the Peace River grain. That particular railway, because it is not an alien railway and because it is owned by the CN and CP jointly, has the use of these hopper cars.
In 1975-76 another 4,000 were bought by the federal government. In 1978 another 2,000 were purchased. That is 8,000 altogether. As we all know, the minister now has a commitment which was made by the former Conservative minister to purchase another 2,000 cars. Even though there is some doubt about that commitment, since he is using different criteria to make an assessment, I understand from the answer he gave the other day to one of my own friends from Alberta that he will live up to that commitment. So the federal government will have about 10,000 of these cars in service. These are allocated to the national railways at a cost for maintenance and repair of 3 cents per mile.
It is true BCR has been offered some of those cars but 23 cents a mile was demanded for maintenance and repair, and that is not tolerable. It is true, also, that British Columbia has not contributed to the extent of other provinces to the aquisi-tion of these cars. Alberta has made a commitment to purchase a thousand cars, and other provinces have purchased or leased some. On the other hand, the government of British Columbia will have told the minister during his visit out there that it has made contributions in other areas, namely, through the development of Prince Rupert, helping with the infrastructure to a large extent, and so on. So there is no excuse for the withholding of a number of these cars which are owned by the taxpayers of Canada through the Wheat Board. There is no reason a portion could not be allocated to the British Columbia Railway, and I hope tonight the parliamentary secretary will have an answer for me.

speakeroldname: Mr. Robert Bockstael (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: TRANSPORT-MOVEMENT OF GRAIN-ALLOCATION OF HOPPER CARS TO BRITISH COLUMBIA RAILWAY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad of this opportunity to reply to the hon. member on this question of the allocation of hopper cars to the British Columbia Railway.
The hon. member suggested that BCR is viewed by Department of Transport officials as a foreign railway. The fact is that the railway does not come under the Railway Act and is therefore not obliged to carry grain at the Crowsnest Pass rates. I am sure our major railways find this position enviable. The British Columbia Railway voluntarily maintains a rate structure for grain comparable to the statutory rate.
May 6, 1980

It is correct that no hopper cars purchased by the federal government or by the Canadian Wheat Board have been allocated to the British Columbia Railway. This is because of the general shortage of cars and the fact that the federal government has no jurisdiction over the said provincial Crown corporation. However, the government is sympathetic to the case presented by the Peace River region grain producers that the railway which serves them should receive an allocation of hopper cars from the federal government and the Wheat Board fleet.
The Wheat Board has entered into discussion with the British Columbia Railway to establish the railway's need for the cars. As the hopper car fleet increases, so does the likelihood of some cars being allocated to the BCR for grain service. Nevertheless, the federal government must obtain certain assurances from the railway regarding car operation, future rates to be charged and grain service provided.
I am pleased to inform the hon. member that discussions have taken place as recently as this morning between the Canadian Wheat Board and the British Columbia Railway and that it is very likely some agreement will be arrived at in the near future.

Mr. Speaker, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) indicated on his return from Washington that he had received no commitments from the Americans. In fact Mr. Costle, the head of the Environmental Protection Agency, said the following about planned coal plants in the United States: If the coal plan means more emissions in the northeast, "we are going to have to offset them," meaning the emissions, "somewhere else."
Where is that? Are the Americans considering setting aside some areas of their country as pollution wastelands? Is Canada to be one of those zones, or is this government going to be tough and aggressive and protect this land and Canadians?
The minister alluded to the fact that ten years ago the Scandinavian countries were concerned about acid rain. Today their lakes are dead. What the minister is saying is that we will cut back a few percentage points over the next few years while the United States increases by many. The remedy the minister offers is a prescription for a dead environment. Why has he not taken the reins in this situation and set acceptable limits to be met this year, in time to be of some use to Canada?
The U.S. response is unacceptable, and it is time to increase pressure from Canada. The Liberal actions are a peculiar approach: on the one hand to export low-cost non-polluting natural gas to the United States while, at the same time, President Carter is putting in place and operating coal-fired plants with little and often no pollution reduction equipment. There is a need for analysis of the costs foisted on us by the Americans, and at the same time an analysis of the energy
Adjournment Debate
benefits given to the United States by our country such as hydroelectricity and natural gas.
Our lakes, buildings, farms and health are taking the brunt of coal-fired pollution to allow the coal-producing and consuming states to maintain low energy rates and costs.
The United States is dumping five times as much on us- three million to four million tons per year-as we are on them. They dump about one quarter of their airborne pollution into Canada, which kills off lakes, etc., in Ontario, Quebec, and the maritimes principally. Quebec is one of the most sensitive geologically, and the history of the federal government in pressuring the U.S. has been weak-kneed and ineffective.
Destruction of the Canadian environment by "insignificant increment" now has deadlines that can be measured in tons, days and months.
The minister made political hay here in Canada recently by juggling maximum limits from Inco, which were at 3,600 tonnes per day and, with present output, are only 2,200 tonnes per day. This allowed the hon. gentleman to lull Canadians into thinking that something is being done and that because Inco was not polluting full bore the minister was somehow responsible for this incremental reduction. This is hardly the case. Available information in Canada indicates that emissions can be brought by Inco to below 1,000 tonnes per day at a cost of only 20 cents per pound. This would put Inco in a highly competitive and unreduced production position. Why is the minister not mobilizing a plan to reach the figure immediately?
The question is, what is the minister doing? I state to the House that he is doing nothing in Canada to demonstrate a tough attitude in order to protect Canadians from our own pollution, nothing to demonstrate to the United States that we will stop dumping over one million tonnes per year into their back yard, and nothing to awaken the United States to the fact that Canada will not accept the destruction of our environment, lakes, fish, farmland, health, forests and genera! wellbeing. In fact President Carter proposes to increase emissions by hundreds of thousands of tonnes into Canada.
Is the minister waiting for a major health epidemic or photographs of thousands of dead acres of fish and trees? Or is the de facto Liberal policy that the environment is of no value?
Perhaps the minister's representative here in the House tonight will reveal just what steps the Liberal government and the minister are taking on all fronts to obtain reductions from the United States. If he cannot be specific, that is precisely what he should say to this House and to Canadians.

speakeroldname: Mr. Roger Simmons (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Science and Technology and Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding what the hon. gentleman has said about acid rain in the Scandinavian countries, acid rain has not long been recognized as a problem of major proportions. Indeed, it was only in 1976 that the OECD recognized it as a serious problem. It is only in the last half dozen years, I say to my colleague, that the matter has

May 6, 1980
Adjournment Debate
appeared to take on the kind of urgency which he speaks of tonight.
In those years the problem has mushroomed in Canada. We now emit into the air in sulphur dioxide and nitric acid something in the order of five million metric tons of the first, sulphur dioxide, and just about two million metric tons of the latter, nitric acid or nitrogen oxides generally. It is a problem of major proportions. The problem is seen in its true proportions when we realize that the United States emits five times what Canada does.
As I listened to the hon. gentleman, I realized that much of his grievance is against the United States, and so is ours. To that end about three weeks ago the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Roberts) went to Washington and spoke with Mr. Costle, the head of the Environmental Protection Agency, about the subject of acid rain and what ought to be done about it.
We are very disappointed and discouraged by the failure of the Carter administration to include any provision for reducing emissions in its coal conversion program. However, I say to my friend, the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton), that the light at the end of the tunnel is that Mr. Carter's coal conversion program has not yet passed the Congress. I say to him, and to others in the House, that this is a good time for us in the House and in the country to give a higher profile to the
increasingly serious subject of acid rain and its adverse environmental impact on acquatic life and, to some degree, though more indirectly, on agricultural products.
There are things which we have to do here at home, and to this degree we wanted to be identified, as we were last week, with the program being undertaken by the Ontario government in so far as Inco in Sudbury is concerned, but that is only part of the solution to the problem. It is easy to knock it because we have not come up with an instant solution in one day, as is the wont of my colleague and his friends in that party, but we are on the road; we are beginning.
Part of the solution lies in persuading the U.S. government and the U.S. Congress that what they are doing with the coal conversion program without proper safeguards in so far as acid precipitation emissions are concerned, is further damaging our situation here in Canada and their own situation in the United States. I believe that that is the main lever which, without reference to partisan causes, we should highlight now to the degree that we may have some effect, we hope, on the passage of this coal conversion program through the American Congress.
